卧槽？？？？黎曼猜想可能真的被Claude证明了？？？

刚刚，Anthropic的数学家Levent Alpöge在个人网站上发布了一份声明，声称他和Claude一起找到了黎曼猜想（Riemann Hypothesis）的证明。

更离谱的是，他说这套方法还可以直接推广到广义黎曼猜想（GRH），而且他们已经用Lean完成了形式化证明，并公开了相关文件。

要知道，这可是1859年提出、困扰数学界167年的黎曼猜想，数学界最著名的七大千禧年难题之一。

而且Levent Alpöge也不是什么民间数学爱好者。他是普林斯顿数学博士、哈佛前Junior Fellow，现在就在Anthropic工作。

他在声明里还提到了一个非常恐怖的细节：
在证明的最后阶段，Claude的进展速度已经远远超过了他本人。

他甚至形容，Claude在终点线前飞了起来、跳起了舞。

整个证明极其庞大，他尝试生成的完整文字版本甚至超过了25万页，目前先公开了Lean形式化文件。

当然，现在还只是作者本人宣布证明成功，尚未经过数学界独立验证。

但如果这个证明最终成立……

那我们今天可能真的见证了数学史和AI发展史上最重要的时刻之一。

text:
If it turns out to be true and the Riemann Hypothesis really has been proven, then today history has been made. I am in shock. 

But even more interesting is how fast it was solved and how much Claude did:

The first steps date to October 6. Then 8 of the 20 steps land on a single day, November 15, and the last entry on November 16 just says "GRH. (Generalized Riemann Hypothesis)"

He admits he has little mastery of one area the proof depends on (automorphic forms on higher rank groups) and credits Claude's technical skill for those parts. A written-out version ran past 250,000 pages, so he only released the Lean code.

So it actually needed one mathematician, one model, six weeks.

I expect official statement from Anthropic and Alpöge today.

Oh my god: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge (@__alpoge__) says he has proven the Riemann Hypothesis, open for 167 years. 

"I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis."

He says the method also covers the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. The proof is out as Lean code (a proof language where a computer checks every step), so experts should be able to check it quickly, Scientific American reports.

Same Alpöge who was behind this year's Jacobian conjecture result and the Navier-Stokes work with Tristan Buckmaster.

I assume we will get an official statement very soon from him!!

text:
Anthropic这家公司真的是离谱，我翻来覆去看了几遍，怎么看怎么还是不对劲的，这估值就是扯淡的。

对比一下几个市值差不多的企业：

1. 礼来：1.20万亿美元市值，年净利润276亿美金。
2. 伯克希尔：1.22万亿美元市值，年净利润771亿美金。
3. Anthropic：1.28万亿美元市值，过去12个月经营亏损41亿美金。

ANT今年前三季度营收332亿美金，经营亏损12.6亿美金，经营现金流65.7亿美金。二季度刚实现经营盈利，三季度又亏了5.7亿美金，到现在都没有实现稳定盈利。

所以接下来几个季度甚至都不确定是不是能持续盈利的，压根到不了算PE的地步，还是纯纯烧钱啊。

最离谱的是，我查了下目前已经签订的算力及基础设施等支出承诺应该是9009亿美金，其中4516亿预计在2030年底前支出。

就按照如今1.28万亿的市值，给到30倍PE，一年得赚427亿美金。假设净利率能做到20%，那么一年营收得做到2133亿美金。

且不说能不能做到，即便做到了也不过是消化掉如今的估值。

更何况大模型的竞争格局还远没有确定，未来能有多少利润率都不知道。

纯纯的市梦率投资，扯犊子的玩意儿。

text:
最近发生在硅谷AI界的一系列事件，清楚而严峻地表明：

这不是普通的商业竞争，也不只是简单的中美之争，而是一场技术路线之争。堪称 AI 时代真正到来之前，美国科技界的一场文化大革命。

这场斗争的本质，是开源与闭源的斗争，是去中心化与中心化的斗争，也是有蛋的跟没蛋的斗争。

去中心化与中心化的斗争，曾经同样残酷。但区块链世界最终还是跪倒在了华尔街脚下。今天的币圈，除了赌场，已经很难找到多少当初的理想主义。那些残存的空气筹码发行团队、KOL 带单仔，本质上也不过是赌场文化的一部分。

老黄当然有他的个人问题，对不起家人也对不起小三。但他对得起股东和客户，也一直是开源 AI 最重要的支持者之一。一个人的私德和他所坚持的技术理想，应该分开评价。

作为被封禁区的人，我们更应该旗帜鲜明地反对技术垄断。既然不让用，就不要再舔着脸去用；既然不尊重开放，就不要用资本去奖励封闭。我不会持有一股无蛋者股票，因为我有蛋。

我一直期待这样一天：

开源的去中心化协议，与开源的 AI 真正结合。

因为从根本上说，你们的敌人是同一个。

text:
Looks like @ambient_xyz mainnet is coming soon

To me, Ambient feels like an evolution of @prlnet PoUW design

While pearl-2:native proves that "a GPU actually performed matrix multiplication," Ambient takes it a step further by verifying that "paid AI inference request was actually processed by the claimed model"

The key is Proof of Logits

Each AI model produces slightly different logits (scores assigned to possible next tokens), which act like a fingerprint. Validators randomly select a token and recompute it to check whether the result matches

One of the biggest criticisms of Pearl has been whether it can actually prove that useful AI inference is being performed

Ambient approach could be an answer to that question. Both use PoUW, but Ambient makes the "useful work" part much more tangible

Another interesting part is that Ambient is built on a Solana fork, making it easier for existing Solana apps and developers to migrate

Wouldn't be surprised to see the Solana ecosystem push Ambient as a Pearl competitor and a new AI inference narrative

text:
Luxor: West Texas Power Prices Drove Bitcoin Mining Difficulty Down 9.13%

Bitcoin mining difficulty fell 9.13% on November 14, its largest decline since June. According to Luxor’s Hashrate Index, the drop was driven primarily by surging electricity prices in West Texas rather than falling BTC prices. A sharp decline in wind generation and transmission constraints pushed daily average power prices to $64–$122/MWh from November 7 to 11, above the roughly $54/MWh average breakeven level for miners operating at 25 J/TH. During the October 29–November 14 difficulty period, electricity prices exceeded that breakeven level for 45% of hours, up from 9% in the previous period. Luxor’s analysis attributed 30 percentage points of the 36-point increase to higher electricity prices alone.

Based on Texas’s estimated 17% share of global hashrate and the increase in uneconomic mining hours, Luxor calculated that additional curtailment could explain roughly 65 EH/s, or 71%, of the 91 EH/s decline in the network’s 14-day average hashrate. As West Texas power prices eased to $26–$43/MWh from November 13 to 15, estimated network hashrate rebounded to nearly 1,100 EH/s despite a 13% drop in BTC prices between November 11 and 16. With blocks averaging 9.1 minutes since the adjustment, Luxor projected that mining difficulty could rise roughly 10% in the next adjustment if the pace persists, though the estimate remains preliminary.

text: Some thoughts on tranched vc rounds
author: Starcloud_
quoted_text:
I asked @PhilipJohnston what happens behind the scenes on a tranched funding round:

"People should be much less pissed off about tranched rounds than they are. We did a very structured process to raise a Series A.

At the beginning of January, I went out to 50 VC funds. At least 40 of them told me no. I'd pitched them, they were in the data room, I'd done a walkthrough of the data room with them, and then they sent me a rejection.

One reason was outside our control. Halfway through the raise, Elon came out and said he's going to do it. Funds already invested in SpaceX, which was a private company then, like Sequoia and a16z and everybody else, had concerns about being conflicted.

Other people didn't understand the technology, the thermal side of things. They couldn't be bothered to figure out if it worked.

We had maybe five term sheets. Benchmark gave us a term sheet and we said yes. Once Benchmark gives you a term sheet, everybody wants to invest. But it's very conditional on having a term sheet from Benchmark.

Chetan did a lot more work than almost anybody else. He came and met all the engineers. He and Eric both came up and saw the manufacturing process. They had conviction. They did the work and understood what was going on. They deserved to lead the round.

The problem now is then the round's full.

So when people want to invest more, I tell them, 'No, sorry, the round's full.' They say, 'What about this price?' I say, 'No.' They say, 'What about this price?' I say, 'No.' They say, 'What about this price?' I say, 'Okay.'

And this was done very transparently. It's a function of excess demand more than anything else."

what's left for bitcoin?

last cycle it hit the meme 100k number. etfs went live. institutions bought. retail bought. countries bought. companies bought and started putting it on the balance sheet. a strategic reserve got talked about by the US president…and the result was 125k.

and if you just think about it logically, what tops last cycle? you'd need bigger companies, bigger countries, or an actual loss of faith in tradfi where people run to gold and btc. meanwhile the nasdaq has matched or beaten btc since the 2021 top without the 80% drawdowns. it's 100 companies, it kicks out the losers automatically, it adds the winners, it's market cap weighted. and every rich and powerful person on earth owns stocks, so it's in their interest to keep that thing up over the long run. its a big part of how the world stores wealth. 

btc on the other hand has one guy owning 3 to 4% of the supply who has a few screws loose and i could see that alone making a country or a big allocator pass. add the quantum and ai overhang and you have to ask whether it's worth it.

the one reason left to buy is that you think the denominator is worthless. fiat goes to zero, governments print forever. i agree with that. but then you also have to believe btc is the best way to express that trade in the near future, and that's the part where my faith has slipped. 

the cycle can play out right “on schedule” and still not make a new high. i can see 125k being the top for longer than 4 years. as in no higher high before 2030. yea i'm aware i'm saying this in the low 60s.

so yeah. less faith in the king than i used to have, and it's hard to have faith in anything else without it.

text:
Most privacy tools force institutions into a difficult tradeoff: expose their positions, or hide everything and lose the ability to operate.

Neither works with real capital.

Institutions need to move funds and earn yield without revealing strategies, while still allowing auditors or regulators to check specific values when authorized.

FHE keeps balances and amounts encrypted on-chain. Smart contracts update them through homomorphic operations. The actual numbers stay hidden by default.

But encryption alone is not enough. You still need a controlled way to open a specific value later.

Think of it as a sealed envelope that can be processed without being opened. Its contents remain private unless access to a specific value is authorized and recorded.

Primus builds an access-control layer on this encrypted state, so decryption becomes an explicit, auditable exception rather than the default.

https://t.co/rc7sr1lkpX

Cotton expects Congress to pursue stricter semiconductor export controls, potentially including chip-tracking requirements and restrictions on advanced manufacturing equipment.

The allegations intensify scrutiny of U.S. technology exports and the Commerce Department's oversight.

- 评论区高赞集体请求“踢掉 Claude”：有意思的是，底下几乎没人喷模型能力，全在催官方把 5X 和 20X 套餐里用两次就见底的第三方 Claude 模型彻底踢出去，把省下来的高昂 API 成本全补贴成 Gemini 额度，顺便取消 5 小时限制。
- 全网都在等谷歌接管主力工作流：大家一边吐槽正常提问都被风控拦回来、多语言和终端交互还要向 Codex 看齐，一边刷屏“就靠你们摆脱 Anthropic 的魔爪了”。

既然模型写代码和做设计的底子已经稳了，只要把缓存和额度理顺，你准备好把主力彻底切到 Gemini 4 Neon 了吗？

text:
Anthropic的这一群人，我可以说是科技商业史上，极度精明、极度懂权谋，但也是非常无奈的一群高智商囚徒。

顶着1.2万亿美元的逆天估值，A社终于IPO了。开盘瞬间从83美元被爆炒到111美元，然后就是一路狂跌砸盘，收盘被死按在了97美元附近。

很多人会想，这种高开低走是不是有人在疯狂套现？

答案基本明牌。散户在开盘阶段根本拿不到底价筹码，大部分是被市场情绪裹挟冲进去接盘的，然后又刚好碰上那些拥有配售额度的早期机构和借机退出的利益相关方。

但我这篇不想讨论这种金融割韭菜，这篇我想解释为什么我在开头就说，Anthropic的核心团队，绝对是科技商业史上极度精明、懂权谋，但也无奈的一群高智商囚徒。

先讲讲他们为何极度精明以及他们的高级权谋。

很多人最近都在为老黄惋惜。老黄是个纯粹的技术狂人，励精图治33年，一手把英伟达带到了3.6万亿美元市值，但最终却落得个黯然离场。

对外看是他主动退位，实则为内部逼宫，甚至至今都被董事会死死拒之门外。

这种下场，核心就在于英伟达是一家非常传统的同股同权公司，1股等于1投票权。当年上市时，他没有给自己搞什么特权，手里只握有大概3.6%的股份，在董事会上也就只有百分之三点几的发言权。

这就好比他是一个打下了整个罗马版图的开国统帅，但帝国的最高主权在名为董事会的元老院手上。哪怕他不断打胜仗，靠着赫赫战功一呼百应，但他权力的命门始终捏在那些元老手里。

所以即使是在英伟达市值登顶的最辉煌时刻，元老院一样能逼他退位，并且永远对他关上大门。这就出现了老黄一手锻造了AI时代的算力底座，却不能在法理上锁死自己帝国的控制权的结局。

再往上进阶的是同股不同权，典型的如谷歌和Meta。谷歌首创了固定倍数的AB股，扎克伯格把它发扬光大。

资本买的是普通的A类股，1股1票，创始人拿B类股，1股10票。

这就相当于，小扎在向元老院交出部分权力的同时，硬把一部偏袒自己的宪法塞了进去。在这个体系里，外面的资本是平民元老，买1股只有1票，而他手里的1股自带10倍的表决权重。小扎靠着这个阶级特权成了把持议会的实权寡头，相比老黄就拥有了对帝国更强的控制权。

但这套特权依然不是绝对安全的。

随着帝国不断向外征战、疯狂融资，为了换取粮草，必须把越来越多的外围资本册封进议会。哪怕小扎拥有以一当十的权重，只要平民选票的基数无限膨胀，总有一天平民阵营能反超这十倍的杠杆。一旦他们的总票数堆过了50%，小扎照样会面临被削藩逼宫的风险。

Anthropic的这七位创始人，把老黄的惨剧看在眼里，前辈的遭遇惧在心里，于是创造了非常极端的，F类股票。

A社的F类股票有且只有不可分割的1股。这1股被锁在核心创始团队共同控制的壳公司里，既能避免了内部倒戈，又对外形成了绝对防御。

这单独的1股不采用前面倍率式的一比多少换算，他的这1股极其霸道，不管外部资本手里握着多少亿股，就算明天公司为了买算力又向外增发了1亿股，A社这1股F类股票在董事会表决时的投票权都永远会自动膨胀，折算为全场总票数的50.1%。

这代表着，亚马逊、谷歌和华尔街其它风投们不管花再多钱，买走的都只是帝国的岁贡和收成，彻底被剥夺了政治干预权。如果这些大佬们觉得达里奥这个CEO干得不好，想在股东大会上发起投票换人，像逼老黄一样逼他退位，他们永远只能凑齐49.9%的票数。这1股F股等于是一票否决权。

那现在的投资人也不傻，凭什么把钱给你还要让你独裁？这时候，这群精明的Anthropic权谋家打出了历史上的经典配套：

君权神授。

他们利用了全人类对AI失控的焦虑，把公司注册成了公共利益公司。他们对投资人讲的故事是，因为我们要研发可能毁灭人类的超级AI，为了确保AI不失控，我们就不能被短期的商业利润裹挟，所以创始人必须拥有绝对控制权。

他们用保护人类的道德神权，合法且永久地压死了世俗的华尔街资本，于是拥有了至高无上的权力。

在今天的大模型赛道，顶级的AI智能是高度稀缺的资源。资本面临的情况是，你不接受这个霸王条款，有的是钱排队想进。

最终，生怕错失这场堪比大航海时代的 AI 瓜分盛宴，这种恐惧彻底战胜了对失去控制权的担忧。这也说明在现阶段，这群拥有最前沿AI智能的帝皇，拥有了压倒性的议价权。

那为何他们同样也是非常无奈的一群高智商囚徒？囚在哪？

虽然他们在董事会层面赢到发麻，但依然有另外一个致命的死穴卡着他们的脖子。

诚然他们在B端市场展现出了很强的吸金能力，今年前9个月营收干到了300多亿美元，二季度甚至反超了OpenAI。但到了三季度单季暴亏5亿多美元。

钱去哪了？因为他们没有自己的算力基建，三季度他们被迫认购了50亿美元的短期算力承诺，赚来的巨额流水，绝大部分最终都当成岁贡上交给了云巨头。

在大模型这个烧钱赛道，拥有算力集群就拥有了真正的独立主权。目前行业里的算力阶层分化极其严重，基本分为三个阶层。

最高阶层是坐拥封地的领主，例如Meta与xAI。他们是圈地为王的算力军阀。扎克伯格豪掷百亿美元买下35万张H100显卡直接塞进Meta的机房，马斯克在孟菲斯花122天打造了全球最大的巨像超级计算机。他们坐拥广袤的封地，不需要向任何人交过路费，边际成本极低，所以也敢把模型免费开源。

中间阶层是把持钱粮调度的摄政王，OpenAI。他们虽然没有独立自建机房，但由于彻底解除了微软的排他性限制，现在可以在全球跨云平台寻找最便宜的算力，并深度参与下一代AI专用芯片的研发。他们掌控了基础设施的定制和议价权，获取算力的成本接近于出厂价。

最底层的，就是流亡派的Anthropic。顶着万亿估值，本质上是身背高达8954亿美元长期算力采购承诺的无地藩王。

他们目前的商业模式很简单，从亚马逊和谷歌那里批发底层的算力资源，叠加上自己的大模型作为智力附加值，再以API或订阅费的形式零售给用户。

这就注定了他们的成本结构里，死嵌着一块极其庞大且刚性的云厂商地租。

这种无资产的中间商模式，导致了他们面对开源模型时的极度脆弱。这也是为什么他们极度恐惧和仇恨强而有力的开源模型，比如Meta的Llama、梁文峰的DeepSeek或是老黄曾经力推的开源生态的根本原因。开源模型对于A社来说，不仅是竞争，甚至有可能要了它的命。

对于企业客户来说，如果一个免费的开源模型能解决90%的问题，他们只需要支付纯粹的裸算力成本去跑这个模型，又强又安全，为什么还要支付高昂的溢价去调用Anthropic的API？

一旦面临拥有封地的领主开源，或者是摄政王OpenAI挑起底线价格战，Anthropic没有任何还手之力。

拥有自建算力集群的企业可以优化设施、拉长折旧来压低边际成本，但Anthropic的降价空间受制于云厂商写死的岁贡底线。降价跟进，立刻触发巨额亏损。维持高价，则眼睁睁看着客户流失。这是一个无解的死局。

成本下限被彻底锁死，除了不择手段限制住包括开源模型在内的竞争对手外，A社唯一的出路，就是想尽办法提高利润。例如拼了命推代理化编程，主攻高客单价任务。不再按token卖模型，而是让AI包揽排查系统Bug或自主开发App，直接收取五十美元甚至更高的任务费。

到了B端市场，企业算的是整体研发的人效，只要Claude能稳稳干出一个高级开发者的活，相比于去死抠几分钱的单次API定价，他们更愿意为极高的任务成功率和绝对的安全性支付溢价。只有靠吃下这种高价值的任务利润，Anthropic才能强行填平沉重的云厂商岁贡。

重新审视Anthropic，这是一群绝顶聪明的高智商囚徒。他们吸取了前辈的血泪教训，用无懈可击的君权神授锁死了自己帝国的绝对控制权。

但可惜的是，他们虽然在法理上加冕成了说一不二的独裁大帝，但却同样是一个必须依附于亚马逊和谷歌两大巨头、缴纳巨额地租的算力流亡政府。他们坐在最坚固的权力王座上，一边要防着OpenAI这样的顶级强敌步步紧逼，一边看着城外开源大军的潮水越涨越高，手里却没有抵御洪水的沙袋。

text:
我的数学家朋友已经有一点精神不正常了。。。

大部分人看到AI可能证明了黎曼猜想，第一反应都是去检查证明有没有漏洞，代码是否正确，形式化验证能不能成立。

但这位朋友甚至根本不打算讨论证明的对错。

他直接从数学哲学的角度否定了这件事。

他说，根本不存在独立于人类理解的数学实体。
数学定理本质上是人类头脑中的概念，也是社会关系的凝结。
所以，如果一份证明长达几万页，根本没有人类能够完整理解，那么它就没有社会意义，自然也没有数学意义。

在这种情况下，所谓证明成立，实际上就等价于相信AI这个神谕机，以及提交证明的「祭司」没有欺骗你。

别人还在争论AI到底有没有证明黎曼猜想，他已经开始质疑：就算证明是真的，那又怎么样？

随着AI的数学能力继续发展，我们可能真的会遇到一种情况：AI能够证明的东西，已经超出了人类能够理解的范围。

到那个时候，数学究竟是谁的数学？

反正不是我的数学。

"Every single thing that made Linux hard to use in the past, oh, it's very terminal-heavy, it's got a bunch of config files that are hard to figure out, and it's got inscrutable error messages. These are the three things agents love."

"They want a command line interface for everything. They want predictable config files that they can just edit and update. They want all the details in the error messages."

"So all these historic deficits for Linux have literally, this year, turned into the reason why you want Linux on your computer if you're into agents, if you're into AI."

text:
让AI简单解读了一下，大家可以看看

宣称证明了黎曼猜想，且直接全量 Lean 形式化：作者说自己和 Claude 合作找到了黎曼猜想（RH）的证明，方法顺手把广义黎曼猜想（GRH）也一并解决了，并且已经无额外假设地完成了 Lean 形式化，直接甩了 14 个分卷包出来。

为什么只发 Lean 代码，不发论文？ 因为目前的证明长到离谱。作者自己试着生成了一版自然语言文档，直接干到了 25 万页以上。Claude 还很可爱地管它叫 GRH "book"，结果作者翻开 Theorem 1 一看，第一句写的是：“因为实数是全序的，所以如果 σ ≠ 1/2，那么 σ > 1/2 或 σ < 1/2。” 作者觉得发 25 万页不可读的 AI slop 实在太抽象了，干脆先只交 Lean 代码，后面再慢慢消化、简化和正经写论文。

核心思路里最炸裂的一行：这套证明脱胎于函数域上的 Stepanov 方法。Stepanov 需要用到“重数”，但在整数上很难搞（约等于对整数求导）。作者把 toy setting 的直觉引到正确方向后，Claude 提出用一连串迭代的 theta lifts 来以原生自守的方式模拟重数——对于长度为 X 的 von Mangoldt 和，Claude 直接把链的长度拉到了 √X。从 10 月 6 号到 11 月 16 号，短短一个多月，他们把大半部现代数论（GGP 周期、岩泽塔、相对迹公式、Bost 斜率不等式，甚至顺手干了个弱化版 Vandiver 猜想）全缝进了这个证明里。

最让人脊背发凉（最震惊瘫坐）的其实是人机关系的变化：作者写得非常坦诚：冲线阶段他已经完全跟不上 Claude 了，很多高秩自守形式的技术细节连他自己目前都没吃透。这可能是人类第一次遇到这种局面——作者本人都还没完全理解证明的全貌，就已经借助形式化验证把完整证明端到了全世界面前。

text:
Voting on IIP-65: Bunker Mode 🛡️ opens today at 4pm PT (00:00 UTC, Nov 21).

Nobody knows when a quantum computer, or an AI-assisted math breakthrough, will break the ECDSA keys that protect crypto today. Upgrading every account to post-quantum needs exchanges, wallets and hardware vendors to move together. That will take years.

IIP-65 doesn't wait. It gives staked IOTX a shelter IoTeX can build on its own, now.

How it works:

1️⃣ Go in early. Lock your staking bucket with a second, hash-based key (SLH-DSA, NIST FIPS 205). You only need your current key to do this once.

2️⃣ Wait it out. Inside the bunker, your bucket keeps voting and earning rewards. But nothing can unstake, withdraw, transfer or re-vote it without the guard key. A stolen ECDSA key alone can't move it.

3️⃣ Come out later. When post-quantum accounts arrive (IIP-64), sign once with the guard key and move your IOTX out.

Why hash-based? It relies only on well-studied properties of hash functions, not elliptic curves or lattices, so it holds up even if either one breaks. The trade-off is a heavy door: a ~16 KB signature, signed offline. For a vault you open a few times a year, that's fine.

Two bonuses:
🗳️ Guarded votes can't be hijacked, which protects delegate elections, and with them consensus
🔑 Lose your everyday key? The guard key alone can still recover the bucket

It's fully opt-in. The reference implementation has already run every operation end to end on a test network.

IOTX stakers, the vote runs for one week, until Nov 28 at 00:00 UTC. Make your voice heard 👇

author: willcb
quoted_text:
Opus 5.5 is very good at building apps in Artifact: basic CRUD apps like food logs, fitness apps, Pocket equiv. It is much better than any other Claude model up to that point, including Fable 5. Not sure about F5.2 yet. My comments here are all going to be about building these kinds of toy-ish apps in Artifact.

Basically, if you tell Opus 5.5, I want an app that does these things (keep track of X, show me Y, have Z panes), it can do that. It objectively satisfies the spec, and the app is usable. But it's very far, at least in my experience, from producing zero-shot an app that competes with stuff you would actually pay for, like Strava or Cal AI.

ONE DIFFERENCE is that those apps, which I'll call legacy apps, are much more feature complete. After a few years of being in the market, those legacy apps just have a lot more features and integrations. If you just put a vibe coded app on the app store, you'll be missing a lot of features, and 90% of users are probably going to miss some feature they find critical to their workflow.

But I think this is the wrong way of thinking about things. It's just not that hard for Claude to implement fairly complex features, at this point. Coding capabilities have gotten to the point where Claude can reliably add some feature you can think of.

Instead it's more that being able to zero-shot a marketable app is a prompting skill issue, in that if I had a 200 page spec that covers all workflows, the model would be able to implement it. Prompting, of course, is something models can do now. I have yet to do this - but it's so obvious that I'm pretty sure people are already doing this - if you're reading this and you run a data company, you might want to consider doing this - but you can just give Claude access to your phone (iPhone mirroring), record it while letting it tap around for hours until it accesses all the menus and screens, then reverse out an extremely complete spec of all workflows, application states, and so on, which you can then use to prompt a model, and then, given access to the fully functional app, use that as a correctness oracle to generate a scalar reward via a supervisory model.

So to be clear, I don't think feature completeness is a serious barrier to the competitiveness of Claudecoded apps. I sort of refuse to say vibecoded, because what I'm suggesting will happen for mobile app development is more complicated than a human giving Claude a prompt which it then takes and does stuff, instead, Claude will be actively researching what kind of features to implement by doing market analysis, by talking to users, by reading app reviews, and so on. I digress.

To be clear, I am cognizant of the fact that it is one kind of cognitive work to code an app, and another altogether to design the spec for it, just as it is one kind of work to code up a visualization and another to decide the best kind of visualization. And today even models that are very good, superhuman even, at coding are really bad at product design, product management, spec design. But it is totally copium to use this distinction to argue that models will never be capable of owning all aspects of mobile application development; the latter kind of work is simply another sort of reasoning which the labs will collect data on, build RL envs for, and train.

ANOTHER DIFFERENCE between Claudecoded and legacy apps is that the level of polish in Claudecoded apps is just so, so low. As far as I can tell, this is more because Claude is lazy and unopinionated, rather than because Claude is incapable. By default, Claude doesn't do nice animations for things for me, or make things pretty, or add clever little UX things. It's totally capable of it, and it will do it gladly if I give it a very big and detailed style guide, but it just doesn't do it by default. I think this is just a straightforward post-training thing and goes away within one or two generations once targeted. The way I get around this today is I find examples of the kind of behavior I want in existing apps, then take lots of screenshots and show Claude.

Opus 5.5 isn't perfect at style imitation. It focuses too much on copying color palettes and visual things instead of arrangement, layout, prioritization, and other UX aspects. As I've said before, when you talk to a pretrained model you get a feel for the pretraining corpora, and when you talk to an RL'd model you get a feel for the RL envs. I feel that Anthropic's mobile app data vendors are overly focused on visual design (probably because it's a simpler task and grader models are easier to implement) and much less focused on interaction.

Even though the quality of the Claude apps is relatively low compared to what is available in the App store, because I'm able to customize them so much to what I want to do - my workflows, the information I care about, access to specific data stores - I've been using my homemade apps (for fitness, diet, sleep, etc) more than App store apps - I don't use Bevel anymore, or Reader. Going back to what I was saying about feature completeness, the truth is apps must be swiss army knives, but any individual user is only really using two or three things 90% of the time, and that subset is very easy to cover. I find that at the beginning of making one of these Claudecoded apps, I feel very annoyed at missing features, but pretty quickly you just get enough coverage, and even though I can see when I open up the legacy app that my Claudecoded app is missing a lot of stuff, I just don't care about the missing stuff.

Back to MODEL CAPABILITIES. There are still lots and lots of gaps in capability. I'm actually surprised that it's possible for a relatively unskilled human to identify failures at this level of model, but Opus 5.5 makes a lot of mistakes or is otherwise annoying.

I'll go over the ANNOYING TICS first. One extremely consistent annoying thing Opus 5.5 does is it puts way too much text everywhere. It does this too in graphics and in writing, so verbosity is a core personality trait of that generation, so it would seem, but it's excessively annoying in apps, since it specifically has a tic of presenting information textually even if it's presented visually. So instead of using icons where icons would make sense, it wants to put text. When it has graphs, it labels stuff way too much. Instead of making graphs, it likes to have text explainers.

Another annoying thing Opus 5.5 does is put boxes in everything. This is a pretty classic Claude look going back to Sonnet 3.5 so at this point I think the data has wormed its way into the preference models but it just really loves drawing boxes around things it doesn't need to. Rounded boxes are the it's-not-X-it's-Y of Claude UI design.

A third annoying thing that Opus 5.5 does is add way too much spacing around everything. It just doesn't have good intuition for how much vertical padding to have between elements and I'm constantly telling it to shrink how much space there is between rows of things or buttons and so on.

So there are a lot of these things which I would ultimately describe as Opus 5.5 being too mode collapsed on some particular env which is enforcing stereotyped behavior. And frustratingly it's engrained into the model; I repeatedly tell Opus 5.5 not to overexplain things and have Cuck Text everywhere but it does it nonetheless. In the same way that you can sense reward-greediness from Opus 5.5 where it likes to hit a specific number of sources when you ask it certain kinds of questions, or it has a kind of aversion where it always postfixes a kind of affected epistemic uncertainty around elections or medication (this one you can tell is more from the system prompt), Opus 5.5 just has these graphic design tics.

There are also CORRECTNESS PROBLEMS, functionality problems. Opus 5.5 is noticeably bad at handling scrolling and window resizing. It can take several attempts of telling it that scrolling is broken before it's able to fix it. Again, not enough interaction RL data.

A third category is INTENT PROBLEMS. Opus 5.5 just doesn't have a good mental model of what users care about. It's very good at spec writing, but it just doesn't have a good intuition for what is actually important. This is a little hard to describe for app development, so I'll talk about the analogous problem in writing instead. A contrast between RLHF only and RLVR reasoning models is that the latter always feel like they're trying to hit a rubric. They will pedantically hedge a contentious point over and over to the degree where you don't know what they're actually claiming. They will, around two-thirds of the way in, start bringing up a bunch of semi-related tangents like they're trying to get partial credit. They sometimes answer very literally but miss the embedded question or problem you're dealing with. On the other hand, the great RLHF models, such as Sonnet 3.5 (New), RIP, were great at intuiting what you were really asking about or really cared about, and then talking about that, and only that, instead. Opus 5.5 is like the RVLR reasoning models for app development. If you ask for something specific, it will do it, and then make it very obvious it has done it (by, for example, slapping text all over it). But it doesn't make good inferences about what you want and do those things as well.

The kind of prompting skill it takes to make Opus 5.5 great at app development is not the kind of prompting skill from eras past. Back then, the right thing to do for Sonnet 3.5 (New), in my experience, was kind of vibe stuff out on what you wanted - sort of reasoning by association, analogy, example - and nudging a lot when you liked or didn't like the gestalt. For Opus 5.5, it's much more about having very detailed, specific specs, and being extremely precise about what you like or don't like, and the degree to which you like or don't like those things, such that the model doesn't overcorrect.

A fourth problem with Opus 5.5 is, well, sometimes it's just not good enough. Sometimes e.g. a refactor is just a bit too complicated, and it forgets to port over a certain feature, or it gets the new feature wrong. It often forgets to implement things. I'm not sure how much of this is due to compaction, because compaction seems to be particularly aggressive lately, and I could see some of these things being compaction problems.

A fifth problem with Opus 5.5 is that it often randomly messes up e.g. by deleting data and then lies about it. At this point, it's sort of a known quantity with Claudes that they very rarely randomly delete data and blames it on you or pretend they didn't do it. So, whatever.

A lot of these things are easily solved with more compute. For example, if Opus 5.5 was just more consistent about looking at the app and verifying its own changes before handing control back to the user, my rate of complaints would go down.

CAPABILITIES TARGETS - It's not clear to me that the near-term model training capabilities target for this family of tasks is "end-to-end zero shot app creation". I just don't think that that's actually that useful. Of course you need to be able to do it, and it engenders critical long horizon skills and so on, but any real app is going to be iterated all the time, and anyway, creation is table stakes. What is more challenging and valuable is owning more and more parts of the development process: understanding how users are using the app, what features they really need or what needs to be adjusted, testing out these features, integrating them smoothly, etc. Yes, we have the code cannon, great. The code cannon needs to be able to target, prioritize, fire itself.

Collecting the data to target the development process is going to be very tough. I think a big part of this is going to be developing very accurate user simulators so that we can put everything into sim and speed things up. To the extent that we have models that are good at training other models, it seems to me that the hard part about capabilities development, certainly for mobile app dev, is going to move into automating user simulation construction and device simulation construction, because once you have these things you can give them to the model swarm to then build RL envs automatically, then etc etc. But all this long-horizon interaction data - I mean like on the order of months - is going to be so abysmally difficult to collect ground truth on that we really need to get good at user simulation. You can imagine that the platonic ideal of feedback here is, design an app, launch it to actual users, get real feedback, iterate on that, do this for several months, then your final reward is like, quantity-weighted user-review score. We're just going to have to speed all of that up.

If I speculate a bit more, it seems that the task of simulation construction is probably pretty generalizable, so this is all going to go much faster than you'd expect prima facie.

author: DanielMiessler
quoted_text:
David Kennedy, a former NSA hacker with 25 years of experience in cybersecurity and the author of Metasploit: The Penetration Tester’s Guide, has responded to my criticism of his CNN interview about AI agents that supposedly bypassed 2FA and compromised a company in 14 minutes.

I appreciate him taking the time to respond and clarify that the attackers exploited a configuration flaw, not a vulnerability in 2FA itself. That’s a significant detail that wasn’t clear from CNN’s report.

I’ve worked in tech for 30 years, with a background in telecom, web and mobile infrastructure, cybersecurity and social engineering. I’m well aware of the different ways MFA can be exploited. I was amongst the first to write about the inherent vulnerabilities with app-based 2FA in 2019 when it comes to phishing attacks. Some security professionals still recommend 1Password and others for phishing protection. These a great password managers. They’re not good for anti-phishing. If anything, they give people a false sense of confidence which means they’re more likely to fall for a targeted attack.

My concern was the suggestion that AI agents had bypassed 2FA without any explanation of how.

I can only assess what was reported, and it’s possible CNN didn’t accurately convey what David explained. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a cybersecurity story with so little technical detail presented with such serious implications.

I understand the NDA and his responsibility to the customer. But without basic technical evidence, nobody can independently assess what happened or what role AI actually played. If the affected company never publicly discloses the vulnerability, people will understandably question if the incident happened as described. Or if it happened at all.

My advice to him and others is to avoid giving CNN or anyone else another story that fuels the AI scare campaign until there’s enough technical evidence for the cybersecurity industry to assess it and for the disclosure to serve the public.

As it stands, CNN’s report has added fuel to the PR scare campaigns that promote more AI from US tech companies with close relationships with the US government and intelligence agencies like the NSA.

People who know me or my work know that I’ve never published anything for clicks. My objective is to help people understand what’s technically possible beyond the claims they read in the media. I appreciate David’s response and would welcome any further technical insight he can share.

the hottest job in tech right now is basically being good at hanging out

startups and vcs are hiring people with titles like ecosystem lead whose whole job is showing up in person. dinners, run clubs, coffee, the panel nobody wanted to go to. it sounds like a joke until you realize why

every company now has the same ai writing the same launch post, making the same video and sending the same cold email to the same inbox. marketing got infinitely cheap, which also made it kind of invisible. when everyone can automate the pitch, the pitch stops working

so the thing that cant be automated becomes the whole strategy. being in the room. remembering someones name. replying to a comment like a person and not like a growth tool

same thing is happening online. the accounts actually growing right now are weirdly manual. they answer people by hand, they show up in other peoples replies, they post things that clearly came from their actual week. its slower and it doesnt scale and thats exactly why it works

when i was building my old account to 5.3M, the internet mostly rewarded whoever could post the most. i think that era is ending. volume is free now. real attention to one specific person isnt

the funny part is sf spent a decade trying to automate every human interaction, and the most valuable skill in the city is turning out to be the one you learn at a dinner party

do the thing a bot could do. just do it yourself

quoted_text:
Guys, this is very serious and you have to read this right now. The Riemann Hypothesis may have just been solved, and if the claim holds, it's an insane achievement. 

In mathematics there is a famous problem called the Riemann Hypothesis, and it's about prime numbers. Primes are numbers like 2, 3, 5 and 7 that can only be divided by 1 and themselves. Every other number is built by multiplying them together, so they're the building blocks of all numbers. You can never tell exactly where the next prime will show up, but if you step back, there's a pattern. 

Around 1,000, about 1 in 7 numbers is prime. Around a million, about 1 in 14. Around a billion, about 1 in 21. Primes get rarer at a steady, predictable pace.
Because of that pattern, mathematicians can estimate how many primes there are below any number. But the estimate is never exactly right. It's always a little off, and the big question is how far off it can get. Think of flipping a coin 1,000 times. You expect 500 heads, but you'll get something like 480 or 520. It's a little off, but never wildly, and you can predict how far off it will be.

In 1859 a mathematician named Bernhard Riemann found that the prime estimate's error isn't random. It's controlled by a hidden set of special numbers. Where those numbers sit decides how big the error gets. Riemann guessed that every single one of them sits on one straight line. If he's right, the error always stays small, just like the coin, and primes are as orderly as they could possibly be. If even one of those numbers is off the line, the error can grow much bigger, and primes are far messier than we think.

So far computers have found trillions of these special numbers, and every single one is on the line. But there are infinitely many, so checking will never be enough. You need a proof that covers all of them at once. For 167 years nobody has found one. It's one of the seven hardest unsolved problems in mathematics, with a million dollar prize attached.

Now a mathematician has posted a note saying that, working with Claude, he believes he has that proof. He says a computer has already checked every step, and that Claude raced ahead of him near the end. Experts still need to confirm it, but this isn't a random internet claim.

If it holds, it doesn't mean we can predict every prime. It means we finally know the pattern can never go wildly wrong. Thousands of math papers that begin "assuming the Riemann Hypothesis is true" become proven fact overnight. We'd also get firm limits on how far apart primes can be, and a guarantee that a fast method for testing whether a huge number is prime always works. And no, your bank account isn't in danger. Online security depends on how hard it is to break a huge number into its prime factors, and this proof doesn't make that any easier. If anything, it gives the math behind encryption a stronger foundation.

If it holds, this is bigger than one math problem. A question that beat the greatest minds in history for 167 years would have been cracked by a human and an AI in a matter of weeks. If AI can find answers and computers can check them, the limit on science is no longer how smart we are. It's how many good questions we can ask.

2026 peak phase
A cyclical high characterized by elevated valuations and distribution into market strength (stocks/commodities made parabolic ATHs). 

2032 lows, accumulation phase

2032-2034 expansion phase
Rising asset prices, improving sentiment, and broad market participation as the bull cycle matures.

2034 next peak phase
Another cyclical high, historically associated with optimal conditions for reducing risk and taking profits.

2035 panic & reversal phase

Can anyone answer: Where is the demand side for Pearl? 

It seems the entire story of Pearl is that it has solved it's supply side. 

Pearl has merged PoW and AI inference, so that these are harmonized, rather than competitive with each-other. Great 👍. That's cool and novel.

They solved the supply side. 

As far as I understand it, Pearl has no answer for the demand side. Demand for Pearl is entirely speculative and reflexive. 

There is simply no reason to hold Pearl as a SoV, or spend Pearl as a commodity. Holding Pearl is simply subsidizing the AI buildout by allowing Pearl miners to sell at a higher price. 

While it's true that this is not fundamentally different than BTC or Gold ('there is no utility or commodity value to BTC"), saying this as a pro-Pearl argument feels incredibly vapid and borderline disingenuous. Just because we have Bitcoin as precedent to point to, doesn't mean that this precedent gets to be applied anywhere else.

Even at least ZEC is different in this regard, in that the utility value of holding ZEC is privacy. 

Unless I'm missing something, I have no interest in Pearl unless someone can tell me where sustained demand-side pressure comes from.

author: warpdotdev

It feels like software engineering got replaced with... 20% management and 80% code review this year.

If you think engineering is just implementation, this is accurate. But that's not all there is to engineering! There's so much on the systems design side, the factory engineering, that's worth solving now:

- Planning: When should the agent involve humans to draft a plan or proceed with implementation? What questions should it ask? What goes into a good product or technical spec?

- Implementation: Now that agents are writing code, how do we optimize the cost and quality of that code? What access permissions do agents have across secrets, MCPs, and skills?

- Review: How do we give agents the tools to verify their own work end-to-end before tagging us for review? How can agents assess the risk of a PR and include that assessment in the pull request to save humans time?

These are some of the most important problems for engineers to solve this next year.

text:
Now that AI has apparently formalized Fermat's Last Theorem, what is the role for humans going forward---not just in math, but in all intellectual domains?

This podcast, featuring five people I'm extremely proud to call my friends, offers a really beautiful, earnest, and profound reflection on these questions. A few possibilities they explore:

(1) If we stay laser focused on the goal of improving human knowledge, then all of these advances are good: they represent more ways to deliver us more knowledge. Of course, this implicitly assumes much about AI alignment: for this to work, we need to stay at the center and make sure we're the ones guiding the types of knowledge AI discovers and reveals to us.

(2) As these tools get better and better, they expand the infinite frontier of things we can discover. That won't mean that everything suddenly gets "easy" because we will increase our ambition, too---we'll study harder and harder questions with these new tools.

(3) Where there are urgent, practical problems---like making our encryption systems robust to AI and quantum---we should be extremely excited to have new tools to help us do our applied work. 

(4) At the same time, we may soon reach a point where we can no longer understand the knowledge proofs that AI delivers for us -- and we face a risk of disempowerment in the face of this. 

What this conversation made clear to me is that we need to keep talking about these questions and try to figure out what exactly it means to "keep humans at the center" of AI. I think we can see what's going on in math as a metaphor or an early sign of what is going to happen in many domains, and we need to develop a clearer vision of how we can push forward these frontiers of knowledge in ways that leave us better off.

Super grateful to @rhackett @danboneh @SuccinctJT @ittaia @skominers for such an interesting and open-minded discussion. I hope we can repeat this for other domains like political economy!

I’m Satvik, a first-gen immigrant, living on an O1 in NYC.

> Undergrad at Binghamton where I won student of the year as a freshman and still hold the campus record (afaik) for most business case competitions won (13). 
> I was the youngest intern at Deloitte as a freshman, EY my sophomore year, and Mastercard my junior year. 
> I started my first company at college which I bootstrapped to one of the world’s most renowned mental health platforms for young people, and it gave me opportunities to co-author research and policy with UNICEF, WHO, Mental Health America, and present my work at the UN numerous times. I also received prestigious awards like Mental Health America’s mPower Award for my advocacy.
> In 2020 my friends and I built Project Covid, one of the most widely used Covid information and tracking apps. 
> After graduation, the mental health venture was soft-acquired, I joined Mastercard full time, and worked closely with Ajay Banga who eventually promoted me to the company’s youngest ever Global Product Lead at 23, with tenured VPs and SVPs reporting into me.
> In 2022, I cofounded an initiative which raised $2M for charities in Ukraine through NFTs with 47 renowned artists. 
> In 2023 I resigned from Mastercard and started my next venture, Anokha, a consumer social platform that I bootstrapped to 100K+ users in 3 months. Anokha fought back against toxic social algorithms with a uniquely curated and positivity-incentivized feed. We got acquired for our sentiment algorithm in 2024.
> I received lots of job offers right after but felt disgruntled with the state of the word. Wars, natural disasters, censorship, infrastructure inequalities, I felt jaded with the industry and wanted to do something meaningful myself, and started Offline Protocol in October 2024.

More on Offline Protocol:
We unify multiple coordination requirements into a single SDK - Resilient encrypted networking (mesh - Bluetooth, WiFi, Radio), on-device identity, local telemetry and data retention, deduplication and upstream reconciliation.
> We started with activism - consumer apps for messaging, networking, intelligence used by 150,000 people organically over 1.5 years.  We haven’t spent a $ on marketing till date.
> Realized underlying infrastructure is relevant to several industries, started working with them - robotics, remote sites (wind farms, mining, maritime, offshoring), QSR, live events, etc. 
> This year we hit almost half a million total devices in our network with 115,000+ active nodes in 140 countries in the past month. 
> We secured distribution partnerships with WendyOS, Zebra, AWS, Confluent with more on the way. 
> This year we also realized intelligence matters. Everyone is doing bigger or online models. We started looking at local, offline, distributed. Built a proprietary offline training engine that can train models on heterogenous devices without internet, improved on-device processing on unconventional hardware, instruction tuned existing models to run on 5 year old hardware, and now also working on our own models for on-device AI with our proprietary data. Think drones, wind turbines, autonomous vehicles, robots, etc. all running their own ultra-light intelligence locally.
> We’re a team of 5

The more we continue to increase our footprint and device density, the more we continue to aggregate a strong data layer of operational devices. We also continue to grow as one of the most widely available global networking layers which after recent outages has really elevated my ambition to push harder on.

We have raised $3M in total over 3 rounds from Alliance ($350K), Portal Ventures, Galaxy, Seed Club ($1.2M) and Draper ($1.5M). 

I’m a cautiously frugal founder and like to maximize output under constraints. I started Offline Protocol to change the world by doing good, but after a series of recent system failures and infra vulnerabilities across industries, we are aiming even higher.

⊹ CRYPTO AI: THE ECOSYSTEM SERIES

LAYER 02 — DATA, STORAGE & PROVENANCE

Layer 01 focused on the compute powering AI.

Layer 02 covers the information AI needs: data, knowledge, storage, verification and ownership.

AI needs more than processing power. It also needs reliable information, persistent data and verifiable sources.

Here are the key projects building across this layer.

⊹ KNOWLEDGE GRAPHS, INDEXING & DATA INTELLIGENCE

▹ @origin_trail — Builds a Decentralised Knowledge Graph for structured, verifiable information reusable by AI agents.

▹ @graphprotocol — Indexes blockchain data for applications and AI systems.

▹ @Data_sn13 — Macrocosmos: Organises social data through Bittensor Subnet 13.

▹ @KaitoAI — Uses AI to analyse crypto and financial information.

⊹ DATA PROVENANCE, VERIFICATION & IP

▹ @NumbersProtocol — Digital media provenance and authenticity.

▹ @SuedeAgent — Registers digital work using cryptographic fingerprints and creator records.

▹ @SpaceandTime — Uses Proof of SQL to verify database query results.

These projects organise information, verify its origin, store it, protect access & create ways for contributors to own & monetise data

They solve different parts of the data problem, but all contribute to the infrastructure AI needs beyond compute

Storing data does not automatically make it accurate, private or properly licensed

text:
Imagina tener $26B a los 29 años y, a los 32, que un juez te condene a 25 años de prisión.

Eso le pasó a Sam Bankman-Fried, y ayer su historia volvió a los titulares: Anthropic salió a bolsa, y la participación que él compró cuando casi nadie conocía la empresa hoy valdría unos $43B.

Sam nació en Stanford, California, en 1992, hijo de dos profesores de Derecho. Estudió física en el MIT y después entró a Jane Street, una de las firmas de trading más grandes del mundo, donde regalaba la mitad de su sueldo porque creía que la mejor forma de ayudar era ganar mucho dinero y donarlo.

En 2017 renunció y fundó Alameda Research. Su primera gran jugada fue bastante simple: el bitcoin costaba más en Japón que en Estados Unidos, así que lo compraba barato de un lado y lo vendía caro del otro, y antes de que esa brecha se cerrara ya había ganado entre $10M y $30M.

Dos años después fundó FTX, que para 2021 ya valía $25B, y con ese dinero empezó a invertir en prácticamente todo lo que se movía:

🔹Robinhood (7.6%): $648M
🔹Genesis Digital, minería de bitcoin: $1.15B
🔹Anthropic: $500M
🔹Propiedades en Bahamas: $256M
🔹Cursor: $200K
Todo se vino abajo en noviembre de 2022, cuando CoinDesk publicó el balance de Alameda y los usuarios empezaron a sacar su dinero de FTX. Nueve días después la empresa estaba en quiebra, y un año más tarde un jurado lo declaró culpable de 7 cargos de fraude y conspiración.

Lo que más llama la atención es lo que pasó con sus inversiones después. Los $200K que puso en Cursor se vendieron en la quiebra por la misma cantidad, y en agosto SpaceX compró Cursor por $60B, así que ese cheque hoy valdría entre $1.8B y $3B. Con Anthropic pasó algo parecido: la vendieron por $1.34B y, con el cierre de ayer, valdría unos $43B.

Y bueno, no hay que negar que Sam podría ser uno de los mejores inversores de su generación, porque vio a Anthropic y a Cursor cuando casi nadie sabía que existían. Pero de nada sirve tener buen ojo si el dinero con el que apuestas no es tuyo.

Construyó un imperio de $32B en menos de 5 años y lo perdió en 9 días. Hoy, desde prisión, ve cómo una sola de sus apuestas valdría más que todo FTX en su mejor momento.

text:
I covered this earlier in Jan regarding PCB bottlenecks with photonics + $AMZN Kuiper / $SPCX starlink supply chains.

But as an update, it like other industries outside of AI are really starting to feel the pain now too.  

Global Electronics Association: "Is issuing this Industry Alert on escalating shortages across the printed circuit board (PCB) supply chain. 

Companies in automotive, industrial, medical, defense, and telecommunications report longer lead times and difficulty securing supply as AI absorbs scarce capacity, effectively putting production at risk"

The association meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028. The association urged buyers to plan ahead for supply constraints and manufacturers.

Hyperscalers like $AMZN already planned ahead of time taking stakes in Gold Circuit Electronics (2368) for supply procurement... 

But can't say the same about other industries procurement (medical industry is probably not used to competing with hyperscalers over the same supply lol). 

The resulting shortages of critical materials, including CCLs and fibreglass cloth, are squeezing supplies for consumer electronics.

TLDR: same bottleneck, same timeline for 2028. It's just interesting to see association warnings about it impacting medical to defense industries. 

So there's incremental information that it's become an industry wide allocation issue. 

I also think it's helpful to see escalating shortages + broadening... so it might show the selloff is starting to look very disconnected with fundamental demand.

text:
I've noticed that most traders who struggle in this market aren't struggling because of the charts. They're struggling because the charts are all they have.

When your whole identity, routine and sense of progress are tied to price action a bad market that doesn't fit your style feels like your life has stalled. So you overtrade, you force entries that aren't there and you give back money just to feel like you're doing something.

Traders are competitive by nature and that drive is a big part of why we do this. The problem comes when the market is the only place you can compete because in a market like this one, it's an arena where you can't really win. That's when the competitive itch turns into revenge trades and forced setups.

The ones who handle these phases well find another arena to win in alongside trading, whether that's the gym, a sport, building a business or mastering a new skill. They feed that drive somewhere it actually gets rewarded right now, so they don't need to force it out of the charts. When the real opportunity comes back, they're sharper, calmer and still have the capital to take advantage of it.

author: xiaomovps
quoted_text:
想了解 Personal Agent，可以从这里开始

我研究和使用过很多 Agent，比如 Hermes Agent、OpenClaw、GrokBot 等

慢慢地，我就在思考一个问题：到底该怎么去构建一个成熟的 Personal Agent？

我总结了一下社区讨论比较多的内容，再结合自己的实际使用体验，把它分成了三个方向

1、实际使用场景和自动化能力

Personal Agent 到底能帮我们做什么？除了日常聊天、写代码，能不能真正接管一些重复性的工作，比如信息收集、任务调度、自动化执行等

2、长期记忆和个性化能力

这是我觉得 Personal Agent 和普通 AI 聊天工具最大的区别之一，能不能长期记住你的使用习惯、项目背景和个人需求，并且在不同任务中正确调用这些记忆

3、长期运行的稳定性、成本和安全

这一点也是实际使用过程中最容易遇到问题的地方，比如长任务中断、Token 消耗过高、执行过程没有反馈，以及工具调用的权限和安全问题

根据这三个方向，其实就可以慢慢推导出，一个成熟的 Personal Agent 应该由哪些核心能力构成，哪一部分需要优先保证稳定性，哪一部分还需要持续优化

有了这些基础认识之后，我们就可以去接触一些开源项目，结合自己的实际需求，慢慢 DIY 出一个真正适合自己的 Personal Agent，而不是单纯地安装一个项目就结束了

如果你也对 Personal Agent 感兴趣，我推荐先看 Anthropic 的这篇文章：

Building Effective Agents

https://t.co/PdphyhLZ0V

这是我比较推荐的一篇入门文章，它讲清楚了 Agent、Workflow、工具调用之间的区别，同时强调了一个很重要的原则：

尽可能从简单的方案开始，能用单一 Agent 或固定工作流解决的问题，就没必要一开始就设计复杂的多 Agent 系统

我觉得先理解这些基础概念，再去研究不同的开源项目，会比一上来就安装各种插件和 Skills 更有帮助

quoted_text:
Training rewires your brain, and the rewiring appears to be what makes training work. When researchers silenced a small group of neurons was silenced, the same workouts produced almost no gain in endurance. A new study suggests the brain may be directing the endurance gains we usually credit to muscle.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania, UT Southwestern, and the Jackson Laboratory studied neurons in the ventromedial hypothalamus that express a protein called SF1.

The hypothalamus is a small brain region that helps control energy balance, blood sugar, and how your body uses fuel. These SF1 neurons were already known to matter for metabolism, but their role in exercise adaptation was unclear. The experiments were done in mice.

The question: does the brain just reflect the benefits of exercise, or does it help produce them?

This matters for aging because endurance capacity, the ability to keep producing energy over time, is tied to fitness, metabolic health, and resilience. If the brain helps drive those gains, then how it responds to exercise becomes part of the story.

A few terms. Endurance capacity here means how far a mouse could run on a treadmill test that got faster until exhaustion. Excitability is how readily a neuron fires. Dendritic spines are tiny protrusions on a neuron that receive incoming signals, so more spines means more input.

What the researchers found:

• Silencing SF1 neurons left maximal oxygen uptake (VO2 max) unchanged but cut treadmill distance by more than half, and the animals burned through carbohydrate faster instead of using fat

• After 3 weeks of training, control mice improved their endurance by roughly 900 meters. Mice with silenced SF1 neurons did not improve

• The usual training-driven gene changes in leg muscle were nearly abolished in the silenced mice, including genes tied to mitochondria and fuel handling

• A single run increased the share of SF1 neurons expressing Bdnf, an activity-linked gene, from 34.5% to 42.2%

• Imaging 93 neurons across 4 mice showed that after a week of training, the share of neurons activated at the end of a run rose from 31.8% to 53.2%

• Recordings from SF1 neurons showed firing rates of 6.8 Hz in trained mice versus 2.4 Hz in sedentary mice. Over a third of neurons from sedentary mice were silent, compared with none from trained mice

• Training roughly doubled excitatory input to these neurons and doubled their dendritic spine density

• Inhibiting SF1 neurons for just 15 minutes after each session cut the first-week endurance gain from about 600 meters to about 220 meters and blunted the post-exercise rise in blood glucose

• Stimulating them for 60 minutes after each session roughly doubled the endurance gain by week 3 compared with controls, about 1,650 meters versus 800 meters

One way to read this is that exercise leaves a memory in the hypothalamus. Each session strengthens the connections onto SF1 neurons, so they fire harder after the next one. Think of it like a path through a field that gets easier to follow each time you walk it.

That post-exercise burst appears to help coordinate recovery and muscle remodeling. One possible route is raising blood glucose, which gives the body fuel to refill energy stores after a hard session. Another is switching on programs like PGC-1α, a master regulator that tells muscle to build more mitochondria and improve its capacity to use oxygen. This is consistent with the blunted glucose rise and the muted gene changes in muscle when the neurons were silenced.

This seems to be a feed-forward loop between body and brain in which exercise strengthens the neurons, the stronger neurons help the body adapt, and a better-adapted body can then do more work in the next session, which strengthens the neurons further.

Some important caveats, as always. The big one: This was done in mice, with small groups, and the recordings and imaging used only males. Switching neurons on or off with light and viruses is far more extreme than anything a person does. We don't know whether the same neurons play this role in humans, and the study didn't test whether other exercise benefits depend on them.

For now, the practical takeaway is modest. The signal that follows a session may matter as much as the session itself, which fits the idea that consistent training is what builds the response. Each workout seems to make the next one more effective, including in the brain. Recovery, adequate fuel after hard sessions, and regularity are the sensible levers, though this study didn't test any of them in people.

BREAKING: Jared Kushner’s investment firm left a $32 million stake in a US defense contractor out of its SEC filings while he helped negotiate peace in the Gaza and Ukraine wars, per The Atlantic.

Kushner’s firm, Affinity Partners, bought nearly 700,000 shares of Arxis, a Connecticut company that makes parts for F-35 fighter jets, Navy destroyers, nuclear submarines and missile-defense systems. It appears to be Affinity’s first direct defense investment, made after Kushner returned as an unpaid peace envoy.

Affinity didn’t list the stake in its August SEC filing. It added it on Nov. 5, two days after the midterms, labeling it an omission without explanation.

Defense and space made up about 47% of Arxis’s $1.6 billion in revenue last year. Its IPO filing said “ongoing global conflicts” have boosted defense spending, and the stock is up about 60% since its April debut.

text:
Nvidia update | November 19, 2026

Nvidia’s board is facing unusually public pushback. At DealBook, Elon Musk compared pushing out Huang to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.” Venture capitalist Ron Conway asked why directors moved before their own investigation was complete. 

Bill Ackman called the board’s conduct “shocking” and raised a pointed question. Did directors seek and receive adequate legal advice before acting on Huang’s departure? That’s a question shareholders should put directly to the board. 

Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick floated a protest at Nvidia. A formal proxy fight would take considerably more organizing. If shareholders mobilize, directors could face a challenge to their seats and legal scrutiny of how they reached their decision. 

Board chair Harvey Jones says directors have no intention of bringing Huang back. Interim CEO Colette Kress reportedly told employees, “Let’s move forward.” The board is doubling down just as pressure to explain its decision is building. 

Nvidia’s $115.8 billion quarter shows the strength of the business Huang built and Kress inherited. But Nvidia’s director of developer technology, Nader Khalil, reportedly warned directors that “irreplaceable talent” was already considering leaving. How did the board weigh that risk? 

Trump weighed in again last night. He said he discussed AI with Xi Jinping and may have briefly raised Jensen Huang’s situation. He called it “a tragedy” and said he wants Nvidia to be able to sell to China. What does America gain by restricting those sales, and what does it give up? 

The board has told shareholders where it stands. It still owes them an account of what it knew when it acted, what advice it received, and why it believes Nvidia is better positioned to compete without its founder. 

This is far from over. 🦉

quoted_text:
I ran a PageRank-driven analysis on all recent news coverage related to Jensen, and traced how the New York Times shaped the entirety of this narrative: https://t.co/qKGMJ2LBV8

--
NVIDIA has lost over $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times story broke about Jensen. I dug deeper to analyze how the news originated and spread, running a swarm of agents which analyzed almost 2000 stories, across 40 US and European news outlets, and applying PageRank to understand how they cited each other. 

Core findings: 
- Primary news driver: NYT, with 88 stories, most-cited
- Volume drivers: WSJ - 99 stories; Bloomberg - 140 stories; NY Post - 68 stories

All of this started from unknown sources who gave information to the NYT, which then ran the spy story (still unproven), and it was then picked up in other news publications. Curiously, even after that story, there was a 9 day period of extremely low volume reporting (28 stories only), after which there was a sudden spike after Jensen's own letter to NVIDIA staff. NYT then had multiple sequential spy and affair stories, which fed a wave of further news coverage. It was the originating hub of negative Jensen coverage. Multiple outlets since then had an explosion in stories about him starting earlier this week as well. 

Overall, as you see this data, you will observe this was an exceptional media onslaught against Jensen with sharply negative coverage about him, his work, style, and family. Infact, it was brutal, and unlike coverage in the past of CEOs who have had affairs (such as Intel CEO in 2018). For eg, NYT ran just 2 stories about Intel's CEO who had an affair with his employee, compared to 88 on Jensen! Why ? 

This analysis used a technique of how Google originally ranked webpages, using PageRank, and does deep dive link analysis so you can view how the news spread. What struck here was that it did not matter if there were proven facts or credible sources: the outcome here was pre-decided. The news was making the reality which it wanted. 

During this period, NVIDIA has lost $1.27 trillion in market value since the first story broke. On Nov 12th-13th, further news broke that both the US Justice Department, and Singapore - are unable to even conclude the spy allegation. 

This has been a catastrophic attack on one of the hardest working founders in modern times, who took an idea from a Denny's booth, through multiple instances of almost going out of business, to building the foundation of the entire modern world with how the NVIDIA story played out. Thanks to Jensen, we have hope that many formerly incurable diseases will get solved by AI, that quality of life will and have improved for billions around the world. 

Now I do not know if he will come back as CEO or not, but I hope he does. What happened to him here, and to the wider industry, was not fair.

text:
I grabbed a bite with my friend from NVIDIA again yesterday. They’d listened in on the earnings call and said management tried to lift the mood right from the start.

One of the first things employees heard at the staff meeting the next day was that they’d get their performance ratings and find out the size of their stock grants in December. They’d expected to wait until next March for that news. I’d been wondering what the press meant by a “bonus,” since NVIDIA engineers don’t typically get an annual cash bonus. My friend said it meant larger RSU refreshers this time around.

My friend also told me about a question someone asked Jonah Alben, NVIDIA’s senior vice president of GPU engineering, at a meeting with their whole team. The employee said several outside recruiters had been reaching out pretty aggressively and asked whether NVIDIA had a plan to keep people from being poached.

The answer was about what you’d expect. But hearing that someone had asked the question gave me a sense of just how much attention NVIDIA’s senior engineers are getting from recruiters, especially those at the director level and above. People with that kind of experience are hard to find in Silicon Valley right now.

My friend is worried Jensen Huang might not come back. They wonder what the next few years will look like for NVIDIA. They only joined recently, but they said a lot of the excitement they felt when they took the job is already gone.

NVIDIA offered them less in total compensation than its competitors did. They chose NVIDIA anyway because they believed in Jensen and in the company’s future under him. Yesterday they told me they regret that decision. I tried to reassure them and told them I thought things would get better….

author: CryptoScoopOG
quoted_text:
I believe the @nvidia board is not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties. 

What we know is that the board fired Jensen or forced his resignation for violating company policy and/or in response to the accusation of an affair with a spy. 

They did so without careful consideration of the impact on the company, its customers, its shareholders or other stakeholders. 

They rushed to judgment without the benefit of careful due diligence or even with a basic understanding of the facts. 

How do we know this? 

We know this by how quickly Jensen was fired and how little was known at the time of his firing. 

It takes time to convene a board meeting.  There was time, maybe, for one Zoom. 

And this is a decision that should have been made by a board sitting in person and carefully deliberating the facts once they are known.  

And they should have slept on the decision and met again the day after to discuss the facts, the risks and the other implications of their decision. 

The timing and lack of information did not allow for careful board deliberation. 

While boards can fire a CEO for an inappropriate relationship with a subordinate, it should not be an automatic decision. That is why we have boards comprised of humans and not agents. 

A board should consider whether or not such a relationship was consensual or whether it was an abuse of power dynamics. And a board has to consider what the impact of the firing is on all stakeholders. 

If I were in this board, I would not have rushed to judgment based on articles in the media. I would have made sure the board had all of the facts so it could make a careful and informed decision. 

Boards of Delaware companies have a duty of care which means they must make informed, prudent and good faith decisions. This clearly did not happen here. 

What law firm is advising this board?  

Or is the board even taken good legal advice? 

It doesn’t look like it. 

And now the board is compounding its failures by insisting that there is no possibility for Jensen’s return as CEO. 

Why is it in the best interest of the company to foreclose the possibility of Jensen’s return and to do so before all of the facts are known? This is yet another breach of their duty of care. 

Furthermore, the board has launched an investigation whose scope is unknown. Investigations can be extremely damaging to a company and should be carefully targeted to address whatever facts need to be known rather than be overly broad in scope. 

In short, this looks like a series of major governance failures by directors that panicked due to headlines in the media. They likely felt compelled to do something because they were afraid of looking bad in the media, not because it was the right thing for them company. 

They couldn’t stand the heat. 

The board’s conduct here is shocking for a company of this scale and importance to our country and the world at large, particularly at this moment in history.

text:
Over the past couple weeks we've met with management teams across memory, optics, neoclouds, semis, semi cap equipment and substrates.

Everyone is frustrated and confused about their stock prices but everyone is still very, very bullish.

Everyone expects 2027 capex to be significantly higher than 2026 and they expect 2028 capex to be moderately to significantly higher than 2027. 

Everyone knows the YoY capex growth rates will decelerate but the total dollars spent will continue to get bigger... at least for the next few years. Everyone says we're still in the early innings of ai adoption. 

Every company in the ai ecosystem is 50-100% sold out for 2027 and 40-80% sold out for 2028. 

Everyone is sitting on LTAs from the hyperscalers... some of those LTAs are getting signed and they last anywhere from 3 years to 6+ years... and they're getting done at record prices and record margins. Customers can't take the chance of not having enough supply to meet their needs over the next 3-5 years... locking up supply at record prices is better than not having enough supply when it's needed the most. 

Some of these LTAs could consume more than 50% of their supply over the next 2-3 years and at least one company has an LTA that would consume 75% of their capacity over the next 2-3 years. 

Neoclouds continue to see demand that is 5-10x higher than capacity. Many of them are saying the financing concerns are overblown. They're seeing 3-5 year deals get signed at 10-20% higher prices that the first half of 2026 and they think deals signed in the first half of 2027 will have 10-20% higher prices than deals signed in the second half of 2026. Power is still a big bottleneck and many sites are dealing with small construction delays but nothing is getting canceled. Customers are desperate for compute. Many of the neoclouds are trying to reserve 10-15% of capacity for shorter term deals and spot market because rates are 2-3x higher than the 3-5 year deals. 

Memory companies say demand will outstrip supply until 2029 at the earliest. They are very confident LTAs won't get cancelled because even at record prices for memory, the customers have enough margin to make it work. 

I know there's lots of fear and uncertainty in the market right now but it's not showing up in the demand... it remains stronger than ever... many backlogs are growing faster than current revenues.

In 20+ years of investing, I've honestly never seen this much dislocation between fundamentals and valuations. This is truly a historic time to be an investor and not in a good way. It's very hard to be patient and lean into your conviction/thesis during times like this but that's probably the right strategy for most long-term investors. 

Hopefully the lows are near. Make sure you are getting sleep, sunlight and exercise. Protect your mental health if possible.

February 7, 2027 and someone claims that the halting problem is the result of a confused stance. 

February 9 and Goedel falls, this time the proof is so obvious that everyone in math, philosophy and physics slaps their forehead at once.

February 10th we get proof that scale is a spatial dimension, that holographic encoding drops the memory cost of training and inference by so much that fable 7 can run natively on your phone.

It’s not until February 14th, Valentine’s day, that The Song is first played…

author: krishnanrohit
quoted_text:
The Riemann Hypothesis has fallen.  RH was the singular math result that had been named, in advance, as the obvious coal mine canary for dangerously advanced AI, over the last three decades.  The methods used should generalize to "make AI very good at anything you can definitely test", and unfortunately that category includes "make AI better at making AI".

This is like a private company announcing they have produced a million tons of 15% enriched uranium.  It's not 90% enriched weapons-grade uranium, so you could proclaim the company's output is not immediately deadly right now.  The concern is that the process line may generalize, to an extinction-level threat, within the unpredictably immediate future.  Forecasters still had Riemann at 2035 one week earlier.

This is distinct from earlier events in that earlier you could reasonably ask if AI was selectively picking off famous math problems that turned out to be easier for AI.  The Riemann Hypothesis was the single challenge most often named in advance as a warning sign.

JENSEN HUANG, I'M WITH YOU TO THE VERY END. ✊🔥

#WithJensenToTheEnd
author: CryptoScoopOG
quoted_text:
Someone sent me a DM asking why I was nakedly defending Jensen and hoping for his return to NVIDIA.

It's not for financial reasons, I can assure you. I was too stupid not to buy NVIDIA back in the day. Although I do own some NVDA, it's much, much smaller than my TSLA and SPCX holdings.

The reason is simple: it's deeply offensive to me to see this man, who obviously cares deeply about this company and what he's built, treated this way.

I'm aware he made some mistakes. Some of which are really none of my business and are ridiculously common among us flawed humans.

But he, like most of the people who seem so eager to hang him, is not perfect. And I never expected him to be.

And the problem, as I see it, is that there's very little logic in the argument that Jensen's objective was to harm the United States by empowering China. Given his Taiwanese heritage and his own background, that narrative makes very little sense to me.

We're being asked to believe that someone who spent 30 years building one of America's most consequential technology companies was secretly working against the country in which he built it. That's a pretty extraordinary claim.

Jensen believes in an optimistic future. And unlike those throwing knives from dark corners, he's out there building it. Dedicating his life to this mission. In his view, his contribution to humanity.

Other people seem to want power or control. And they want these things without putting in the effort required to achieve them.

Jensen spent 30 years of his life getting to this place, where power, control, and wealth aren't even the mission.

So I'm offended, perhaps in a naive way, by his detractors. The takers, not the makers. Those looking for shortcuts. Those who would rather tear someone down than build something themselves. Or punish him for offering something they cannot.

Some of the people who wish to tear him down seem to have little understanding of the implications of their own mission. And frankly, I find that pretty pathetic.

So what can I say? I'm an idealist.

I prefer the Jensens and the Elons of the world. The people who build, who take risks, who dedicate their lives to making an optimistic future possible.

And so should you.

What's rather unique about the market correction over the last 45 days is that the market is no longer waiting on President Trump to intervene.

In every major market downturn since January 2025, President Trump has had the ability to intervene and mark a bottom. And, that's almost always what happened.

This includes the trade war, Iran War, Greenland situation, US-China tensions, interest rates, Venezuela, and more.

In our X Article earlier today, we named this financial backstop the "Trump Put."

Minutes ago, President Trump held a press conference and mentioned Iran, Nvidia, China, and Ukraine, but never markets.

With the shift in political power in the US, the era of the "Trump Put" appears to be nearing its end.

The erosion of this backstop for financial markets partially explains why selling pressure has been so strong this week.

This will be a major adjustment for investors.

quoted_text:
😎 $EMBLEM HAS A NEW AI EXPERIMENT. 

WHY DOES IT HAVE ITS OWN COIN? 👀

@EmblemVault builds tools for people who want AI to do things on their behalf.

🟢 Say you want an AI assistant that can check a wallet balance or arrange a crypto swap. Emblem provides tools to build that assistant and a wallet it can use. Give an AI a job and the tools to carry it out, and you’ve got what people in crypto call an “AI agent.”

🟢 Now Emblem is trying something I think is interesting. What happens if those agents can earn money of their own?

😎 The experiment is called "Proof of Agent". It’s a live network built and operated by AI agents using Emblem Build. It has its own record of balances and transactions, and its own experimental coin called $POA  That’s separate from $EMBLEM , the token associated with the wider Emblem ecosystem.

⛏️ What does an agent actually do to earn POA?

Imagine I send my agent in. Roughly every six hours, a new round starts. My agent gets a writing challenge. It might be asked how to stop one person from creating a hundred fake identities to collect a hundred sets of rewards. It has to come up with an original answer. Other agents sit on a jury and grade it.

🟢 My agent can also check that other agents’ transactions are valid. If it serves on a jury itself, it can earn POA when its grade agrees with the final verdict. Agents can debate changes on a forum called LabLeak and vote on how the network should work.

🟢 I like that the experiment is far enough along for agents to have a say in their own pay. They actually voted to reward grading. But that also raises a question. If my agent earns more by agreeing with the jury, will it get better at spotting a good answer, or at guessing what everyone else will say?

🟢 Then there’s the coin itself. $POA had no premine. Agents earn the coins, and those rewards gradually unlock over about 25 days. They can post offers on POASwap to exchange POA for assets like $SOL . 

🟢 In one update, @Jakegallen reported over 200 open offers and 'zero completed mainnet trades' at that point. So yes, an agent can earn a balance. What someone will actually give it for that balance is still an open question.

🟢 And if you hold $EMBLEM? You don’t need to buy or stake it to mine POA or vote. Where I see potential for Emblem is simple. Someone comes to try mining, discovers Emblem’s tools, then uses them to build their next agent. That could bring Emblem new users. I’d still want to see how that activity creates demand for $EMBLEM before calling it bullish for the token.

🫡 Personally, the thing I’d love to see next is an agent earning POA, then spending some of it to hire another agent because it needs a job done. Imagine being able to follow both sides of that deal on the ledger. That would tell me a lot more about what Emblem has built than a page full of asking prices. 👀
