text: physical endurance is largely regulated by your brain
author: nptacek
quoted_text:
Training rewires your brain, and the rewiring appears to be what makes training work. When researchers silenced a small group of neurons was silenced, the same workouts produced almost no gain in endurance. A new study suggests the brain may be directing the endurance gains we usually credit to muscle.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania, UT Southwestern, and the Jackson Laboratory studied neurons in the ventromedial hypothalamus that express a protein called SF1.

The hypothalamus is a small brain region that helps control energy balance, blood sugar, and how your body uses fuel. These SF1 neurons were already known to matter for metabolism, but their role in exercise adaptation was unclear. The experiments were done in mice.

The question: does the brain just reflect the benefits of exercise, or does it help produce them?

This matters for aging because endurance capacity, the ability to keep producing energy over time, is tied to fitness, metabolic health, and resilience. If the brain helps drive those gains, then how it responds to exercise becomes part of the story.

A few terms. Endurance capacity here means how far a mouse could run on a treadmill test that got faster until exhaustion. Excitability is how readily a neuron fires. Dendritic spines are tiny protrusions on a neuron that receive incoming signals, so more spines means more input.

What the researchers found:

• Silencing SF1 neurons left maximal oxygen uptake (VO2 max) unchanged but cut treadmill distance by more than half, and the animals burned through carbohydrate faster instead of using fat

• After 3 weeks of training, control mice improved their endurance by roughly 900 meters. Mice with silenced SF1 neurons did not improve

• The usual training-driven gene changes in leg muscle were nearly abolished in the silenced mice, including genes tied to mitochondria and fuel handling

• A single run increased the share of SF1 neurons expressing Bdnf, an activity-linked gene, from 34.5% to 42.2%

• Imaging 93 neurons across 4 mice showed that after a week of training, the share of neurons activated at the end of a run rose from 31.8% to 53.2%

• Recordings from SF1 neurons showed firing rates of 6.8 Hz in trained mice versus 2.4 Hz in sedentary mice. Over a third of neurons from sedentary mice were silent, compared with none from trained mice

• Training roughly doubled excitatory input to these neurons and doubled their dendritic spine density

• Inhibiting SF1 neurons for just 15 minutes after each session cut the first-week endurance gain from about 600 meters to about 220 meters and blunted the post-exercise rise in blood glucose

• Stimulating them for 60 minutes after each session roughly doubled the endurance gain by week 3 compared with controls, about 1,650 meters versus 800 meters

One way to read this is that exercise leaves a memory in the hypothalamus. Each session strengthens the connections onto SF1 neurons, so they fire harder after the next one. Think of it like a path through a field that gets easier to follow each time you walk it.

That post-exercise burst appears to help coordinate recovery and muscle remodeling. One possible route is raising blood glucose, which gives the body fuel to refill energy stores after a hard session. Another is switching on programs like PGC-1α, a master regulator that tells muscle to build more mitochondria and improve its capacity to use oxygen. This is consistent with the blunted glucose rise and the muted gene changes in muscle when the neurons were silenced.

This seems to be a feed-forward loop between body and brain in which exercise strengthens the neurons, the stronger neurons help the body adapt, and a better-adapted body can then do more work in the next session, which strengthens the neurons further.

Some important caveats, as always. The big one: This was done in mice, with small groups, and the recordings and imaging used only males. Switching neurons on or off with light and viruses is far more extreme than anything a person does. We don't know whether the same neurons play this role in humans, and the study didn't test whether other exercise benefits depend on them.

For now, the practical takeaway is modest. The signal that follows a session may matter as much as the session itself, which fits the idea that consistent training is what builds the response. Each workout seems to make the next one more effective, including in the brain. Recovery, adequate fuel after hard sessions, and regularity are the sensible levers, though this study didn't test any of them in people.

text:
Agree with Arian, this is terrible advice. We do the opposite at Alliance. We set fair valuations before Demo Day for each team (erring on the lower side). Our experience has been that this drives much more VC interest.

The opposite backfires – you can't go really back to a VC and say you're now raising at $20m when you told them the week before you were raising at $40m or more. It conveys extreme weakness, will sink your fundraise, and often outright kill your startup.

It also leads to adverse selection. C-tier funds may agree to a higher val, but S-tier investors are certainly very conscious of price. So now you scared off all the good firms and pigeonholed yourself into working with the bad ones.
author: rriccio
quoted_text:
the single worst piece of fundraising advice I've ever heard given to founders (which is highly pervasive right now, and is single-handedly cause my blood pressure to shoot up) is that the valuation you ask for is a reflection of ambition (i.e. if you don't ask for a high enough valuation, you will be perceived as "not ambitious enough"):

> are you building for the long-term or trying to win a short-term popularity contest? its been long documented on the timeline that raising at too high a valuation too soon can sink your company later on (esp when combined with the deadly combo of raising too little capital to minimize dilution). tl;dr you run a high risk of having an overvalued asset without metrics to match the valuation (even if you've made good progress), and you'll go bust
> note that such advice often comes from accelerators. most accelerators know that their returns will come from the top 10% of the cohort, and subsequently (imo) tend to give blanket advice that optimizes for the perceived top 10% (you are in the colosseum competing against a bunch of other startups). that's to say, a lot of this advice can be self-serving (i.e. it serves accelerators' interests for you to valuationmaxxx on demo day, but it probably won't serve yours)
> VCs that judge your ambition based on your valuation cap (vs actual substantive factors driving decisions for your raise) are probably not VCs you want on your cap table anyway

text:
论打游戏对写论文的正当性和重要性_呼应海德格尔 "Sein zum Tode"

主题：世界被“死亡搁浅”事件摧毁后，生与死之间的界限搁浅了——死掉的东西会留在原地(海滩),BT(搁浅体)滞留人间，而主角的任务是把分裂的世界重新连接起来。

"Stranding" 不是 "standing"(站立)，而是来自动词 "strand",意思是“搁浅”(船只困在岸边无法移动)。鲸鱼搁浅就叫 beached/stranded whale。所以 "Death Stranding" 字面是“死亡的搁浅”——死亡像退潮一样，把一切抛在岸边。游戏中还有 "strand" 作名词指“绳索/纽带”(连接人的线)，这是双关。

即基督教信仰中的“向死而生”“死后重建”"Beached things"(BT,搁浅体)是既未完全死去、也未真正活着的存在，滞留在生与死的边界上。这和基督教人论中“未得救赎的灵魂”状态有呼应：罗马书说的“与神所赐的生命隔绝了”(弗4:18)，灵魂搁浅在中间地带。海滩(The Beach)作为个体与冥河之间的彼岸，几乎是但丁《神曲》灵薄狱(Limbo)的意象重演。

Strand:绳索与连接
游戏结尾引了陀思妥耶夫斯基《卡拉马佐夫兄弟》的“棍棒与绳索”之喻：人类曾用棍棒(武力、支配)维系文明而失败，如今要用绳索(爱、连接)重新把世界捆在一起。Kojima 让 Sam 用“结绳”(strand)重建美国，这对应基督教“和好的职分”(林后5:18-19)——基督使人与神、人与人重归于好。

向死而生
Sam 是“遣返者”(Repatriate)，不断从死亡中回来；推到神学层面，这正是“向死而生”(海德格尔用的词，但教会传统早有原型)：唯有经过死亡、胜过死亡，才有真正的生。复活节的逻辑就是“先搁浅，再说生命”。

游戏融合的"strand"哲学、克鲁泡特金的互助论和赫拉利《人类简史》，宗教元素更多是借用西方传统神学意象而非宣称信仰。

text:
卧槽？？？？今天数学界到底怎么了？？？

就在Anthropic的数学家宣布和Claude一起证明了黎曼猜想之后，美国数学会主席Ravi Vakil突然发布了一份紧急公告：另一位数学家Alessandro Masullo也提出了广义黎曼猜想（GRH）的证明！

最炸裂的是，公告特意强调：
全部由人类完成，没有使用AI！！！

而且这还不是今天临时搞出来的。

Vakil透露，斯坦福数学家Brian Conrad已经研究了这份证明好几个月，提供了大量反馈，原本还打算让作者再花一年时间完善论文，经过更多人的审查后再正式公布。

结果现在直接提前公开了草稿，希望全世界的数学家一起来检查、补全可能存在的漏洞。

也就是说，困扰数学界167年的问题，居然在同一天出现了两份声称可以解决它的证明。

一份由Claude深度参与，一份声称完全由人类独立完成。

当然，目前两份证明都还没有得到数学界的最终确认。

但这剧情真的越来越离谱了。。。

人类数学家和AI，居然可能在同一天冲到了黎曼猜想的终点线前。

quoted_text:
The Riemann Hypothesis has fallen.  RH was the singular math result that had been named, in advance, as the obvious coal mine canary for dangerously advanced AI, over the last three decades.  The methods used should generalize to "make AI very good at anything you can definitely test", and unfortunately that category includes "make AI better at making AI".

This is like a private company announcing they have produced a million tons of 15% enriched uranium.  It's not 90% enriched weapons-grade uranium, so you could proclaim the company's output is not immediately deadly right now.  The concern is that the process line may generalize, to an extinction-level threat, within the unpredictably immediate future.  Forecasters still had Riemann at 2035 one week earlier.

This is distinct from earlier events in that earlier you could reasonably ask if AI was selectively picking off famous math problems that turned out to be easier for AI.  The Riemann Hypothesis was the single challenge most often named in advance as a warning sign.

author: adxtyahq
quoted_text:
Software is converging, we always knew it would.

Everyone told us to do ONE thing and do it well. Many still say it's ridiculous, impossible, stupid.

BUT NOW IT'S UTTERLY OBVIOUS. 

This is the only future in software, whether ClickUp does it or not. Even the software giants are already moving toward this new world order.

I wholeheartedly believe that the only way to peak productivity is one platform that does everything, carries 100% of context, and enables everyone to become 100X. 

And it's only possible with AI. 

AI DOESN'T KILL SOFTWARE. IT CREATES MORE OF IT, AND CONVERGES IT. 

If AI makes software dramatically easier to build, software companies will build MORE software. Not less. Right?

The company that built a tool for you will now build more tools. This will never stop.

Categories blur. Competition increases. Features that once justified an entire company become a small feature addition to an existing platform.

Over a given period of time, this is how it will end: Several massive companies that provide ALL software and ALL AI to their customers.

But building more is only HALF the story.

AI needs to understand your context.

And it needs somewhere to actually DO the work.

That's why AI and productivity software are converging too.

Humans and agents need a shared place to communicate, make decisions, and get things done.

ONE APP TO REPLACE THEM ALL 

A behemoth horizontal platform, infinitely flexible, delivering all core software needs, built with common components, primitives, and services that enable mega solutions and compound speed in delivery of software.

THE ERA OF PERSONAL SOFTWARE

To build the everything app and actually work for everyone seamlessly, we rebuilt the application layers  around the concept real-time personalization based on what you want, and what you don't want.

Personal Software adapts in real-time to what matters to you... how YOU work, entirely PERSONALIZED.

You shouldn't have to become a software company just to run your company.

But you should be able to build anything that your creativity can dream of, and that your workflows require. 

The same boundaries disappearing between software categories are disappearing inside our team.

THE 100X STRATEGY IS WORKING 

Since my last post, we shipped more PRs every single week, compounding in growth and these PRs aren't slop - much of this is systems that literally fixed thousands of bugs and constantly optimizes performance.

We now have SIX 100x builders in seats we call Artisans. 10x frontend engineers becoming 10x backend engineers - and skilled enough to do the product work.

Today's EPIC release was built ENTIRELY by our 100x builders. The video below shows what that actually looks like.

And this isn't just about shipping new things faster.

It's about making the things you already use dramatically better.

We've spent the last few months building LARGE-SCALE SYSTEMS and LOOPS that enable us to build with high quality at lightning speed. This was the mandate BEFORE we built more on the platform.

In September, our user generated metrics for quality hit all-time highs, now 90% of ClickUp customers are happy with quality and performance. 

And in a production comparison this week across millions of sessions, ClickUp now loads 40% faster.

Breadth is NOT an excuse for mediocrity in this next era of ClickUp. If we're going to replace your tools, we have to earn it.

I fully understand that we just weren't there yet for the last mile of use cases.

But now, if you get blocked on anything you want, you can simply tell Brain to build it.

In our early days, we made shipping every week part of who we were.

TODAY'S EPIC RELEASE IS OUR REBIRTH. 

We're back. Except now, we're shipping improvements EVERY SINGLE DAY.

I started ClickUp because nearly losing my life made me obsess about the very limited time we have on this planet.

The goal is to enable creativity, and freedom in how you spend your time.

EPIC productivity. 

💜

text:
A compute market cannot work in the way people think it will work because:
- the number of companies that can correctly transition tenants in a multi-tenant infiniband cluster in an automated and secure fashion is under 10 
- of those companies, the number of companies that can offer a live market the works financially is 1, maybe 1.5.

The vast majority of GPU cloud operators literally do not have the basic capability of doing things like "transition tenants".

Transitioning a tenant is a manual process for them that can take weeks and cost millions in idle time. These operators designed themselves for clusters that only ever had one customer. 

The idea that you will have a wide variety of neoclouds who will operate the GPUs and have a market operator will not operate the GPUs is a fantasy dreamed up by people who have no experience in supercomputing. 

Without this capability, you cannot create a viable forwards curve. Simply brokering clusters from one operator to another, on long term fixed contracts, does not build a forwards curve. There isn't enough transaction data to make it viable.

So instead, index providers are forced to build their datasets off on-demand and spot, who's prices do not represent the vast majority of compute deployed, making it very hard to use them for any form of hedging. Index providers are making a valiant effort, but they need physical settlement of the actual asset they're trying to hedge.

英国 DeFi 监管争议：写代码的人，也要承担金融机构的责任吗？

英国加密行业组织 CryptoUK 呼吁 FCA 明确监管边界，不应因为开发者编写代码、维护协议或参与 DeFi 治理，就自动将其认定为受监管金融服务提供者。

这背后其实是 DeFi 长期存在的一个难题：

如果一个协议由开源代码运行，没有单一机构控制，那么监管责任究竟应该落在谁身上？

我觉得，监管 DeFi 最重要的是区分技术开发者和实际控制金融服务的人。

如果连单纯提供代码的人都承担与金融机构相同的责任，未来谁还愿意继续建设开放的区块链生态？

text:
Crypto feels dead right now.

But in 2021, blockchains took 62% of crypto fees. Today, apps take over 95%.

Need some hopium?

Here are 4 areas of crypto still making real progress:

1. Tokens that buy themselves back

For years, the whole plan for most tokens was "buy it and hope someone else pays more later." Not exactly a business model.

Now Hyperliquid, Uniswap and pump .fun use their revenue to buy back or burn their own tokens. Hyperliquid especially, since it makes serious money from real trading.

That means usage can create demand for the token even when nobody's in the mood to buy. Basically, the protocol is the one buyer that never panic sells.

Unlocks still matter, so check that the buybacks are bigger than the new supply hitting the market.

2. Private AI is becoming a real business

Privacy has become one of the more interesting sectors this cycle, and Zcash is getting a lot of renewed interest.

The one I'm watching most closely is Venice. It sells private AI access and uses part of what people pay to buy back and burn $VVV.

New tokens are still being created faster than they're burned, though, so I'm watching it rather than buying it yet.

3. Wall Street is still moving onchain

About $39B of real-world assets, not counting stablecoins, are already tokenized.

Even with everyone scared, BlackRock and other big firms keep bringing traditional financial products onto blockchain rails. They're not checking the Fear & Greed Index every morning like the rest of us. They're planning for years, not weeks.

4. Stablecoins don't need a bull market

There's about $284B in stablecoins today, and more companies are using them to send money across borders.

Tether, Circle and Stripe are all building around this.

A business paying someone overseas doesn't care what BTC did this week. It just wants the money to arrive faster and cheaper, without a bank calling it "3 to 5 business days."

What I'm doing with this

The Fear & Greed Index is at 12, while these businesses keep building.

I'm lining up projects from these four areas and looking for ones where revenue is growing while the price keeps falling. That's the setup I want to be early on when sentiment flips.

I don't know if that's next month or next year, and plenty of tokens won't make it back. But the businesses are still running.

What part of crypto gives you the most conviction right now?

🚨 BREAKING: @thinkymachines just dropped Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weight model that loops.

RAM limits how large a model can be when running Local AI, but Looping allows models to trade compute time for improved reasoning capabilities, effectively making any model you already have access to smarter, but not necessarily larger.

It is their 26.4B parameter (3.4B active) Apache 2.0 licensed LLM. It has 24 transformer layers, but in inference the middle 12 layers are looped 3 times, effectively running 48 layers on each token. This looping allows more computation per token, enabling the model to often solve problems with fewer tokens generated. The model was trained natively in 4-bit precision and takes up only ~20 GB, so should run on any Mac with 32GB of RAM.

author: markjeffrey
quoted_text:
Here's how the AI bubble bursting will make Elon Musk and SpaceX win.

Let's start with what Democrats figured out.

In the midterms, they won by running against data centers. Bernie Sanders wants a national moratorium. And they understood one thing: AI can't really be regulated anymore. The models are everywhere, many of them are open source, and they run on millions of machines.

But a bubble can be popped.

And today's AI sits on a mountain of debt. The labs lose more money than they make. Big Tech will spend over $800 billion on infrastructure this year, more than their businesses generate in cash. Lenders are getting nervous. Blocking data centers is aiming exactly where it hurts.

I think some of them have run the math, consciously or not.

First, superintelligence is going to become a commodity. Like an operating system. Like Linux. When ten models do the same thing and open source is six months behind, there's no moat at the model layer. Nobody pays a premium for intelligence that can be copied.

Second, value is going to move to infrastructure. Chips, energy, cooling, launch. The ones who own the atoms, not the ones renting someone else's.

And two players stand out. Google on Earth, with its own chips, its own cloud, and twenty years of ad money funding it all. And Elon Musk in space, with SpaceX, which absorbed xAI in February for one reason: to put compute in orbit, where the sun almost never sets.

Third, the two big labs, OpenAI and Anthropic, are the most exposed. Massive valuations, massive losses, rising debt. If the money stops flowing, they could go down.

So the logic is simple: if you can't regulate AI, starve it of capital. And if the American economy, which now leans heavily on that investment, goes down with it, so be it. When your power rests on scarcity, you'd rather have a recession than abundance.

But they forgot one thing.

A bursting bubble doesn't kill a technology. It kills the fragile.

In 2000, the dot-com bubble burst. https://t.co/vAW0rIhzhu shut down. Then WorldCom and Global Crossing went bankrupt. Amazon lost more than 90% of its value. Everyone declared the internet dead.

Twenty years later, Amazon is worth trillions, and the fiber laid by the companies that went bust carries the entire web.

The crash didn't kill the internet. It sorted the winners from the losers. And it handed the keys to the most antifragile.

This time will be no different. The labs living off fundraising will suffer. The ones who own the infrastructure will buy up assets at fire-sale prices and come out stronger.

And the most antifragile of them all is Elon. SpaceX has a business that runs without AI: launch and Starlink. And his bet is compute that needs neither the power grid nor a local building permit.

You can vote a moratorium in every county on Earth.

You can't vote one in orbit.

text:
How Jack Dorsey remade Block for AI. His logic is that at a remote-first company every interaction leaves "some sort of written artifact," and AI makes all of it searchable by anyone.

Block has only three roles and no middle management:

▫️Individual contributor (IC): builds or operates something ▫️Directly responsible individual (DRI): owns the strategy and roadmap ▫️Coach: individual attached to an IC or DRI to "help them master their craft"

So the middle layer that used to pass information up and down isn't needed: "The chain of command and the communication hierarchy were just slowing a bunch of that information down."

text:
Nanocode reimplements the Antigravity harness (exact prompts + tools + code mode) inside its own lightweight runtime/SDK/CLI. You get the same Gemini agent behavior but with nanocode’s subagent primitives: typed contracts, massive parallel trees (million-scale in one process, very low memory), multi-provider mixing, and Code Mode.

agy /swarm is Google’s productized coordinator + named workers + verifier + shared board inside the full Antigravity app/CLI. Higher-level orchestration UI, quota-aware, but heavier and Google-only.

nc is the efficient programmable layer; agy swarm is the ready-made team mode.

text:
不管你是支持还是反对黄仁勋复职，我认为代理CEO Colette Kress事后的发言和处理方式不仅不恰当，也相当没品。

在她上任之后的第一次讲话，当被问及董事会是否正在考虑让黄仁勋复职的时候，她以极其生硬、冷酷、机械的方式来回答：

“黄仁勋已经辞去了在英伟达的职务，董事会也接受了他的辞呈。董事会已经决定，不会让黄仁勋复职。这就是我们的声明，也是董事会作出的最终决定。”

我觉得她如此回答，即便是单纯从公司管理和商业角度来说，都非常愚蠢。

她第一次公开讲话，其实上来就应该先表达对黄仁勋的敬意，肯定他为英伟达作出的牺牲，以及他留下的伟大成就。

她完全应该展现出谦逊的态度，告诉大家，自己只是暂时接过黄仁勋的担子，守住他一手打下的江山。等黄仁勋出席听证会、各项调查水落石出之后，再决定公司的未来。

但她没有，她的态度极其傲慢。第一次公开讲话后，她隔天召开了公司全员大会，然后在会上告诉所有员工，是“时候往前看了，我们行的”。 （let’s move forward，we’ve got it）

一家公司的灵魂人物突然离开了，你却轻描淡写地叫大家“向前看”。

这就好比乔丹宣布从公牛退休后，或库里突然宣布离开勇士，然后公牛和勇士的老板出来说：“没问题的，没有他，我们也行。”

谁能相信会有那么容易呢？大家反而会觉得你们没有敬畏之心，而且也没有丝毫人性。

你可以决定不让黄仁勋复职，但在语言上不该如此绝情。这可是一手创立英伟达并带领它成为全球最高市值企业的灵魂人物啊。即便犯错了，行动上可以让他离职，但语言上应该表达尊重和惋惜。

现在这么干，那些在英伟达工作了多年的骨干和老员工会不会心想，你们对黄仁勋都能如此冷酷无情，更何况是我们？

英伟达必定迎来一场离职潮。

Everything is falling at once. Nasdaq is down 18%, Bitcoin broke below $60,000 and gold lost 9% in a week. When stocks, crypto and gold all fall together, the problem is the price of money.

Tariffs and the Iran war pushed up inflation, and the Fed went from cutting rates to raising them. The 10-year Treasury hit 5.31% in October, the highest since 2002. When the US government pays you 5% with no risk, anything that pays little or nothing suffers. Gold pays nothing and peaked in January. Bitcoin pays nothing and fell next. Tech pays far in the future and held on until October.
Then AI cracked too. The midterms raised the prospect of tougher rules on AI and data centers. Genius Jensen Huang left Nvidia at the worse moment, and the stock is down 22%. Anthropic went up sucked $ out of tech and today collapsed.

What am I doing through all this? Nothing. I am not a trader, I build companies and the cash I have I mostly put on Nasdaq 100 for decades. So I hold and wait. 

But it's awful to see many mistakes done at once. @elonmusk was so right about the deficit. Deficit plus tariffs plus war.

text:
Introducing the Agentic Legal Editor in Genie.

Most AI can write a contract clause but a very few can edit a contract like a human.

Claude Cowork, ChatGPT and most legal AI tools can now make basic edits to a Word file. But the formatting doesn't always survive the round trip: a numbered list restarts, a style drifts, a cross-reference points at the wrong clause. Then you spend the time you saved putting the document back together.

@GenieAI's Agentic Legal Editor works in the file itself:
- It edits your original Word file in place. Numbering, styles, tables and cross-references stay exactly as they were.
- New text takes the document's own styles and defined terms.
- It reads the other side's redlines, accepts or rejects a whole round in one instruction, and writes its own edits as native tracked changes.
- It replies to every comment in its own thread, and adds comments wherever the business needs to confirm something.
- Your pen or Genie's: make an edit by hand, give Genie the next one, then take the pen back.
- Every change is saved as a version, and you can compare any two.

The edits you asked for while everything else stays same.

Check it out here - https://t.co/QpTEerm0KY

text: "The Riemann Hypothesis was the single challenge most often named in advance as a warning sign."
author: Altimor
quoted_text:
The Riemann Hypothesis has fallen.  RH was the singular math result that had been named, in advance, as the obvious coal mine canary for dangerously advanced AI, over the last three decades.  The methods used should generalize to "make AI very good at anything you can definitely test", and unfortunately that category includes "make AI better at making AI".

This is like a private company announcing they have produced a million tons of 15% enriched uranium.  It's not 90% enriched weapons-grade uranium, so you could proclaim the company's output is not immediately deadly right now.  The concern is that the process line may generalize, to an extinction-level threat, within the unpredictably immediate future.  Forecasters still had Riemann at 2035 one week earlier.

This is distinct from earlier events in that earlier you could reasonably ask if AI was selectively picking off famous math problems that turned out to be easier for AI.  The Riemann Hypothesis was the single challenge most often named in advance as a warning sign.

text:
翻译：

今天，我们见证了历史。

多年以后，当人类回望 2026 年，一定会将其视为文明跨越的临界点 —— 从这一刻起，所有人的未来都被彻底改写。

变革的微澜或许始于 2025 年底。随着 Claude Code 的出现，AI 智能体（Agentic AI）第一次变得真切可感。步入 2026 年上半年，演进的节奏骤然加快，模型迭代愈发密集，代际间的能力跃升不再只是冰冷的榜单分数，而是人人都能直观体会的差距。然而，真正的质变发生在下半年：故事的主角不再仅仅是模型本身的进化，而是 AI 所催生的科学洞察、研究成果与解题方案本身。就在今天，这一切迎来了前所未有的巅峰。

OpenAI 率先破局，攻克了困扰人类已久的千禧年大奖难题 —— 纳维-斯托克斯（Navier-Stokes）问题。仅仅几周后，他们又发布了逾 300 道数学开放性问题的研究成果，其中不乏悬而未决数十年的硬骨头。整个科学界为之震动，几乎陷入失语。而今天，Anthropic 将边界推向了更远处：数学家 Levent Alpöge 与 Claude 协同工作，几乎可以确定已经证明了黎曼猜想（Riemann Hypothesis）。

这种震撼很难用寻常词汇去描摹，它既令人难以置信，又深邃得近乎不可思议。如果说此前的一切还只是序章，那么今天，便是超级智能（Superintelligence）降临的铁证。这座矗立了 167 年、堪称数学乃至整个科学界“圣杯”的最高峰，终于被登顶。而它所释放的信号再清晰不过：既然它已攻破，那么其余的未解之谜，也终将相继倒下。

我们都很清楚，AI 模型的演进不会就此止步，今天的成就不过是通往更强智能长路上的一个坐标。既然当下的模型已经能够攻克黎曼猜想，我们便很难想象，下一代模型将会解锁怎样的认知疆域。Dario Amodei 曾预言，AI 极有可能治愈人类面临的绝大多数疾病，甚至终结所有疾病。尽管数学与生命科学分属不同领域，但今天这些突破所展现出的底层范式迁移，正让这一愿景从大胆的构想，加速走向大概率的现实。

2026 年必将作为历史的分水岭被铭记 —— 这一年，技术奇点不再是抽象的概念，而是触手可及的现实；而即将到来的 2027 年，将是奇点以雷霆之势全面重塑现实世界的元年。

此刻的我心潮澎湃，既感震撼，又一时不知该从何说起。但抛开纷繁的思绪，内心深处涌动着的，是一种纯粹的喜悦。

对于我们所有人而言，今天，无疑是历史上最美好的日子之一。
author: Tz_2022
quoted_text:
History was made today. Humanity will look back on 2026 and think: this was the threshold we crossed, the moment the future changed for everyone, forever.

People probably first sensed that something was shifting in late 2025 with Claude Code, when agentic AI became truly tangible for them. In the first half of 2026, things picked up speed. Model releases became more frequent, and everyone could feel the gaps between models and the improvements becoming more and more tangible. In the second half of 2026, however, there was a qualitative leap. It was no longer just the models getting better. It was the insights, the results, the outputs, the scientific solutions produced with AI that became more impressive, and today they have probably reached their absolute peak.

OpenAI led the way and solved the Navier-Stokes problem, a Millennium Prize Problem that humans had failed to solve for a very, very long time. A few weeks later, they published results on more than 300 open mathematical problems, many of which had also gone unsolved for decades. The entire scientific world was stunned, frozen in shock. But today Anthropic went a step further. Levent Alpöge, working with Claude, has almost certainly proven the Riemann Hypothesis. This is, and it’s hard to put into words, incredible and unfathomable. Today, I would say, is the proof of superintelligence. One of the greatest mathematical problems, if not the greatest, unsolved for 167 years, the holy grail of mathematics and science, has fallen. And it follows, and this should be clear to everyone, that all other problems will fall too.

We know that the development of AI models keeps moving forward relentlessly, and that this is just one step on the path to ever better models. And if the Riemann Hypothesis has already been proven today, there is simply no telling what even better models will solve. Dario Amodei said that AI will in all likelihood cure diseases, perhaps even all diseases. And although these are two different scientific disciplines, the significance of these breakthroughs shows that this is becoming more and more likely. 2026 will go down in human history as a turning point, the moment the singularity became tangible. And 2027 will be the year the singularity breaks into reality with full force and full impact.

I am in shock and excitement and I don't know what to think. But deep inside if feel joy. 

This day is one of the best days ever for all of us.

Software is converging, we always knew it would.

Everyone told us to do ONE thing and do it well. Many still say it's ridiculous, impossible, stupid.

BUT NOW IT'S UTTERLY OBVIOUS. 

This is the only future in software, whether ClickUp does it or not. Even the software giants are already moving toward this new world order.

I wholeheartedly believe that the only way to peak productivity is one platform that does everything, carries 100% of context, and enables everyone to become 100X. 

And it's only possible with AI. 

AI DOESN'T KILL SOFTWARE. IT CREATES MORE OF IT, AND CONVERGES IT. 

If AI makes software dramatically easier to build, software companies will build MORE software. Not less. Right?

The company that built a tool for you will now build more tools. This will never stop.

Categories blur. Competition increases. Features that once justified an entire company become a small feature addition to an existing platform.

Over a given period of time, this is how it will end: Several massive companies that provide ALL software and ALL AI to their customers.

But building more is only HALF the story.

AI needs to understand your context.

And it needs somewhere to actually DO the work.

That's why AI and productivity software are converging too.

Humans and agents need a shared place to communicate, make decisions, and get things done.

ONE APP TO REPLACE THEM ALL 

A behemoth horizontal platform, infinitely flexible, delivering all core software needs, built with common components, primitives, and services that enable mega solutions and compound speed in delivery of software.

THE ERA OF PERSONAL SOFTWARE

To build the everything app and actually work for everyone seamlessly, we rebuilt the application layers  around the concept real-time personalization based on what you want, and what you don't want.

Personal Software adapts in real-time to what matters to you... how YOU work, entirely PERSONALIZED.

You shouldn't have to become a software company just to run your company.

But you should be able to build anything that your creativity can dream of, and that your workflows require. 

The same boundaries disappearing between software categories are disappearing inside our team.

THE 100X STRATEGY IS WORKING 

Since my last post, we shipped more PRs every single week, compounding in growth and these PRs aren't slop - much of this is systems that literally fixed thousands of bugs and constantly optimizes performance.

We now have SIX 100x builders in seats we call Artisans. 10x frontend engineers becoming 10x backend engineers - and skilled enough to do the product work.

很遗憾我的一直以来的偶像速溶猪老师亏了这么多（如果没有她主持的ethshanghai我可能不会深入开始探索这个行业有趣的故事），，，现在拥有纯粹密码朋克信仰和去中心化精神的加密native的人越来越少了。速溶猪老师是一位，我知道她的手中坚定持有着ZEC，BTC，ETH这些真正具有价值的crypto，可惜这个行业已经被投机者簇拥，可惜像A\这种公司他妈的还在攻击数学界（25w页黎曼猜想你真以为他是为了数学发展吗？）只为了在ipo后提高自己的市值，甚至我们越来越感受到邪恶的闭源AI对于密码学和加密行业，甚至所有的网络安全行业造成的巨大冲击……大部分人手里的crypto几乎全部腰斩了，我相信这一切会令怀有密码朋克最初理想的人心碎。

text:
Scott Briggs Morrow (1957–2022) was a longtime Seattle homelessness advocate, organizer, and pioneer of self-managed encampments and tiny-house villages. He passed away on April 19, 2022, at age 64 from pancreatic cancer. 

Key Contributions
SHARE/WHEEL & Tent Cities: Co-founded the Seattle Housing and Resource Effort (SHARE) and Women's Housing, Equality, and Enhancement League (WHEEL), organizing church-based emergency shelters and pioneering resident-run tent encampments starting in 1990. 
Nickelsville: Helped launch and organize Nickelsville, a network of self-managed encampments and tiny-house villages built around resident democracy, mandatory participation, and collective responsibility. 
Grassroots Advocacy: Spent decades serving morning coffee to unhoused people in downtown Seattle, pushing for resident representation in city policy, and leading direct-action protests.

Morrow is widely remembered in Seattle as a foundational figure—and sometimes controversial, uncompromising leader—behind the city's sanctioned encampment and tiny-home village models. His work continues through community organizers, family, and advocates carrying on his self-management approach.

Scott Morrow reshaped Seattle’s approach to homelessness over four decades by replacing top-down charity with resident-run self-management, direct action, and grassroots democracy. 

Early Organizing & Foundations

Tenants' Rights & VISTA. After graduating from Whitman College with a political science degree, Morrow started his career as a VISTA volunteer and an organizer with the Seattle Tenants Union, building his philosophy around collective power for low-income residents. 
SHARE & WHEEL. In 1990, he co-founded the Seattle Housing and Resource Effort (SHARE) and later helped launch the Women's Housing, Equality, and Enhancement League (WHEEL). Together, they built one of Seattle's largest emergency shelter networks, partnering with local churches and requiring unhoused residents to vote on rules and manage daily operations. 

Pioneering Tent Cities & Tiny-House Villages

The First Tent Cities. Starting during the 1990 Goodwill Games, Morrow spearheaded Seattle’s first organized, self-governing tent encampments on public land—establishing the model for later sanctioned sites like Tent City 3 and Tent City 4. 
tiny-house villages. Residents built insulated wooden tiny homes, ran security shifts, and governed the communities through weekly democratic votes. 
Nickelsville. In 2008, Morrow helped launch Nickelsville—named after former Mayor Greg Nickels to protest encampment sweeps—which evolved from pink-tent protests into Seattle's first

Methods & Philosophy
Self-Determination Over Charity. Morrow rejected traditional shelter models where paid staff dictated rules to passive recipients. Whenever civic groups asked him to speak, he insisted on bringing unhoused residents to speak for themselves.
Daily Presence & Direct Action. For over 30 years, Morrow served morning coffee to unhoused people on downtown Seattle sidewalks. He also led high-visibility protests—including getting arrested in 1996 for opposing anti-homeless landscaping tactics—and brought busloads of encampment residents to City Hall hearings to demand policy changes. 

Controversies & Fractures
Strict Rules & Ejections. Morrow's model demanded mandatory attendance at community meetings, chores, and political rallies. Critics and former residents argued his leadership was overly rigid and authoritarian.
Split with LIHI. In 2019, following reporting by The Seattle Times showing that more residents had been barred from the Georgetown tiny-house village than transitioned into permanent housing, the Low Income Housing Institute (LIHI) terminated its contracts with Nickelsville and Morrow. LIHI took over management of several villages to implement professional case management and lower-barrier rules. 

The funding for Scott Morrow’s organizations—SHARE/WHEEL and Nickelsville—comes from a mix of municipal contracts, private donations, and fiscal sponsorships, and it is significantly smaller than the budgets of Seattle's larger, professionally staffed homeless service providers.
Because these groups are registered 501(c)(3) nonprofits, their finances are tracked through public IRS Form 990 filings and city/county contract records.

1. Where the Money Comes FrGovernment Contracts (City & County). Historically, the City of Seattle's Human Services Department (HSD) and, more recently, the King County Regional Homelessness Authority (KCRHA) have provided the bulk of their operating funds. Rather than paying Nickelsville directly during its early tiny-house expansion, the city funneled money through larger nonprofits like the Low Income Housing Institute (LIHI), which acted as a fiscal conduit and paid Nickelsville as a subcontractor. 
Private & Community Donations. Both groups rely heavily on grassroots fundraising, individual PayPal/check donations, and in-kind support (such as churches hosting shelters for free and volunteer groups providing daily meals). Some programs—such as SHARE's Tent City 4 in East King County—operate entirely without government funding.

2. Where the Money Goes (and How Much)
Unlike traditional nonprofits that spend most of their budgets on salaried caseworkers and executives, Morrow's organizations kept overhead low by relying on unpaid resident labor for security, intake, and maintenance. **You know, keep it for themselves.**

OrganizationRecent Annual BudgetPrimary ExpensesSHARE / WHEEL~$3.0M – $3.1M (FY2023–2024 IRS filings)Utilities and liability insurance for church-based indoor shelters, portable toilets ("Honey Buckets"), dumpster services, bus tickets, storage lockers, and a small core staff.
Nickelsville~$300K (FY2023 IRS filings)Basic village operations, site relocations (moving tiny houses, kitchens, and shower trailers), utilities, supplies, and a tiny staff (roughly three employees).

3. Financial Friction & The "Missing Money" Question:
Questions about where money goes in Seattle’s homelessness system generally stem from three major controversies involving these groups and the broader regional agencies:
The 2019 LIHI Subcontractor Cut-Off. Between 2016 and 2019, the city paid LIHI hundreds of thousands of dollars per village (roughly $400,000 annually for sites like Othello Village) to cover case management, insurance, and site costs, with LIHI passing a portion to Nickelsville for day-to-day management. When LIHI and the city ended Nickelsville's subcontracts in 2019 over management disputes and resident ejections, those public dollars were redirected to LIHI and other staffed providers. 

Informal Accounting Criticisms. City officials and critics previously accused SHARE/WHEEL of being "loose with their finances" and resistant to standard municipal auditing and data-tracking requirements. In 2017, Seattle shifted millions of dollars away from basic overnight shelters (like SHARE's) toward "enhanced" 24/7 shelters with professional case management, shrinking SHARE/WHEEL's city funding share. 
Broader Regional Agency Audits (KCRHA). Public frustration over unaccounted homelessness dollars in Seattle has largely centered on the oversight agency itself rather than small grassroots camps. For example, a forensic audit of the King County Regional Homelessness Authority (KCRHA) revealed millions in unreconciled public funds and an administrative deficit—issues tied to regional bureaucracy rather than the small operational budgets of SHARE/WHEEL or Nickelsville.

The 2013 review involving Michele Marchand (a longtime SHARE/WHEEL organizer and close colleague of Scott Morrow) centered on a Seattle Human Services Department (HSD) fiscal review of SHARE/WHEEL's books, which later became a major point of controversy over weak municipal oversight.

What Happened in the 2013 Review
The June 2013 Meeting: Because SHARE/WHEEL received over $300,000 annually in city grants, city rules required the organization to submit audited financial statements. 
In June 2013, HSD "fiscal audit specialist" Efren Agmata met with SHARE/WHEEL staff—including Michele Marchand and Lantz Rowland—to review their financial records. 
Neither Scott Morrow nor SHARE's outside accountant attended the meeting. 
The August 2013 Clearance Letter: Following that review, HSD's acting director, Catherine Lester, sent a letter to Michele Marchand on August 12, 2013, stating that the city had completed its review and found SHARE/WHEEL’s books to be in order. **SHADY**

Why It Became Controversial Later
In 2016, public records requests and investigative reporting (notably by Seattle civic blogger David Preston on The Blog Quixotic) scrutinized that 2013 review and exposed major gaps in how both SHARE/WHEEL and the city handled financial oversight: 
Unlicensed "CPA" Sign-Offs: For roughly eight years—including the period covered by the 2013 review—SHARE/WHEEL submitted summary financial reviews rather than full independent audits. Those reports were signed by an accountant named Steven A. Isaacson, who claimed to be a Certified Public Accountant (CPA). State licensing records revealed Isaacson's CPA license had actually lapsed in 1984, meaning he was legally unauthorized to perform CPA reviews. 
Lack of City Verification: Critics pointed out that neither HSD's reviewer (who was not a CPA himself) nor city leadership caught the lapsed license or required a full CPA-certified audit before issuing the August 2013 letter clearing Marchand and SHARE/WHEEL. 
SHARE/WHEEL's Response: When the lapsed license was publicly exposed in May 2016, SHARE/WHEEL's board—while maintaining that their internal books were honest—fired Isaacson, demanded the return of organization records, and hired an accredited CPA firm to re-examine their past financial filings.
Lantz Rowland (1956–2017) was a longtime resident of Tent City 3 (TC3) who moved between living in the encampments and serving on SHARE's elected board and staff. He was a key figure in executing Scott Morrow's administrative and political operations. 

Rowland's Role in SHARE & Tent City 3

Camp Resident & Board Officer. Rowland lived at Tent City 3 for years while holding paid staff roles and serving as an elected SHARE board officer. Because SHARE's bylaws required board members and staff to come from the ranks of homeless or formerly homeless participants, leaders like Rowland blurred the line between camp resident and organizational administrator. 
Administrative & Financial Sign-Offs. Despite Morrow being the driving force behind SHARE, Morrow rarely put his own name on official paperwork. Instead, board officers and resident-staffers like Rowland signed off on legal and financial filings—including SHARE's IRS Form 990 tax returns and the 2013 Human Services Department fiscal review alongside Michele Marchand. 
Political Organizing & Meetings. Described by peers as politically astute, Rowland helped run SHARE's internal governance (such as the weekly Monday night TC3 camp meetings and Saturday SHARE assemblies) and frequently represented the organization at public hearings and City Hall demonstrations. After his death on December 31, 2017, advocates placed his memorial leaf on the 5th Avenue side of Seattle City Hall in recognition of his political work. 

How This Fit Morrow's Operating Model
Critics and former insiders often noted that Scott Morrow maintained tight control over SHARE/WHEEL and Nickelsville's direction while keeping his formal title minimal—relying on trusted inner-circle organizers (like Michele Marchand) and resident-leaders (like Rowland) to chair meetings, mobilize campers to City Hall, and sign off on contracts and tax documents.
Rev. David Bloom—a longtime Seattle Baptist minister, homeless advocate, and frequent ally of Scott Morrow's encampment campaigns—was arrested on September 20, 2024, and charged with child pornography offenses. 
His arrest was unrelated to his homelessness advocacy or organizational finances, stemming instead from a cyber-tip investigation.

1. How David Bloom Was Involved in Morrow's Circle
Faith & Political Ally. Bloom directed urban ministry for the Church Council of Greater Seattle from 1978 to 1997, founded the Interfaith Task Force on Homelessness, and later served as board president for Real Change. 
Tent City & Nickelsville Support. Over decades of Seattle activism, Bloom regularly collaborated with Scott Morrow, SHARE/WHEEL, and Nickelsville—joining camp protests, mobilizing church hosts for Tent City 3 and 4, and even receiving daily city fines alongside Morrow during the early 2008 Nickelsville encampment disputes.

2. Details of His Arrest and Charges

The Investigation: In March 2024, Microsoft notified the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) after a user account uploaded files depicting a minor engaged in sexual activity. Seattle Police detectives traced the account to Bloom. 
Arrest & Charges: Following an interview and search at his Seattle condo—where detectives reported finding over 20 illicit images and explicit search histories on his laptop—police arrested the 82-year-old Bloom on September 20, 2024. 
Prosecution: On September 23, 2024, the King County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office charged Bloom with one count of second-degree dealing in depictions of a minor engaged in sexually explicit conduct and one count of second-degree possession of depictions of a minor engaged in sexually explicit conduct. 
Sacred Heart of Jesus Church (232 Warren Ave N, in Seattle’s Lower Queen Anne / Uptown neighborhood) was indeed one of the central physical hubs used by Scott Morrow, SHARE/WHEEL, and their partner programs. 

How Sacred Heart Was Used
SHARE/WHEEL Shelter & Meeting Space. Sacred Heart Hall served as a longtime host site for WHEEL women's shelters and SHARE/WHEEL operations. Because SHARE/WHEEL deliberately avoided renting expensive commercial headquarters—instead operating out of church basements, the Aloha Inn, and the Josephinum—Morrow and fellow organizers regularly used space at Sacred Heart to coordinate shelter logistics, store supplies, and hold meetings. 
Broader Homeless Service Hub. The parish campus (which also housed the Queen Anne Food Bank and the separate Sacred Heart Shelter run by Catholic Community Services) functioned as a major neighborhood anchor for Morrow's network, alongside other host churches like Trinity Episcopal Parish and First Presbyterian. 
Minimal Overhead Model. Using donated or low-cost church spaces like Sacred Heart allowed Morrow's organizations to keep administrative rent negligible while maintaining a direct daily presence among shelter residents.

Beyond church basements like Sacred Heart, SHARE/WHEEL relied on two major downtown-area buildings—the Josephinum and the Aloha Inn—as operational anchors for intake, administration, and resident-run housing. Both properties were owned or formally operated by Catholic Community Services (CCS), which partnered closely with Scott Morrow's network. 

1. The Josephinum (Downtown Administrative & Intake Hub)
Location: 1902 2nd Ave (accessed via the alley entrance between 2nd and 3rd Avenues, just north of Stewart Street). 
How SHARE/WHEEL Used It: While the upper floors of the historic hotel served as low-income supportive housing run by Catholic Community Services, the basement served as the primary operational headquarters for both SHARE and WHEEL.
Daily Functions: Shelter Screenings & Intake: Unhoused adults showed up in the alley outside the Josephinum basement six days a week (Monday through Saturday) for walk-in intake screenings to get placed into SHARE’s indoor church shelters.
Dispatch & Supplies: It served as the central hub for distributing daily bus tickets, storing organizational records, and coordinating logistics for the decentralized shelter network.

2. The Aloha Inn (Self-Managed Transitional Housing)
Location: 1911 Aurora Ave N (on the eastern edge of Queen Anne, just north of downtown).

How It Started: In 1991, after SHARE members occupied an abandoned Metro Bus Barn near Seattle Center to protest shelter closures, negotiations with the city led to the conversion of a former motel on Aurora Avenue into the Aloha Inn—specifically designed as a 66-bed, resident-managed transitional program.

How SHARE/WHEEL Used It: Although Catholic Community Services held the formal operating contract and provided case management, the Aloha Inn was built on Morrow's self-management model. Residents had to contribute roughly 15 hours of community work per week (running the front desk, kitchen, and maintenance), participate in peer-led house governance, and maintain sobriety. It also functioned as a meeting and organizing hub for SHARE leadership and alumni moving from shelters into transitional rooms. 
3. Scattered Host Sites (Decentralized Model)
Rather than maintaining a single mega-shelter, SHARE/WHEEL used the Josephinum basement to dispatch residents each night to rotating or host-partner spaces across downtown, 
First Hill, and surrounding neighborhoods—including First Presbyterian, Trinity Episcopal, St. John United Lutheran, and Woodland Park United Methodist—keeping central administrative rent virtually zero.

The listed represent a cross-section of Scott Morrow’s inner organizational circle at SHARE/WHEEL and Nickelsville, alongside key figures in Seattle’s broader homeless advocacy, media, and service ecosystem who frequently collaborated with—or sometimes clashed with—his network.

1. SHARE/WHEEL & Nickelsville Insiders 
(Core Leadership & Resident Organizers)

• Peggy Hotes: Morrow’s longtime domestic partner and co-organizer. Alongside Morrow, she was one of Nickelsville’s central behind-the-scenes organizers, managing camp relocations, logistics, permitting, and political strategy—and continued leading Nickelsville projects after Morrow's death in 2022.
• Anitra Freeman: A longtime SHARE/WHEEL leader and former tent city resident who served on SHARE’s board of directors since the 1990s. She was also active in the Women in Black vigils and the Homeless Remembrance Project.
• Jarvis Capucion: A longtime Tent City 3/SHARE board member and Nickelsville resident-organizer. Following Morrow's passing, Capucion stepped forward as a primary public spokesperson and staff organizer for Nickelsville.
• Marvin Futrell (Marvin Futrell III): Started as a SHARE tent city organizer before expanding into regional and national policy—later serving as co-chair of the King County Regional Homelessness Authority (KCRHA) Implementation Board, director of policy for the Washington State Lived Experience Coalition, and co-director of the National Coalition for the Homeless's NW office.
• Beatrice Marius: A resident-spokesperson and organizer within SHARE’s shelter network (including serving as spokesperson for SHARE's Holly House program).

2. Real Change & Media Allies
Morrow’s encampments relied heavily on Real Change—Seattle’s street newspaper—for public messaging, legal coalitions, and vendor recruitment:
• Timothy (Tim) Harris: Founding director of Real Change (leading the paper from 1994 until stepping down in 2020). Harris worked closely with Morrow on encampment relocations, anti-sweep protests, and joint lawsuits against the City of Seattle, though he later broke with progressive advocacy orthodoxy in 2023 over encampment clearings and addiction policies.
• Dr. Wes Browning: A former math professor who experienced homelessness and has served since 1994 as Real Change's circulation/vendor specialist and longtime weekly columnist.
• Neal (Neil) Lampi: Longtime Seattle shelter director and contractor affiliated with Real Change.

3. Broader Seattle Homelessness Movement Figures
Rex Hohlbein: A Seattle architect who founded Facing Homelessness (and the BLOCK Project, which places tiny homes in residential backyards). While both championed tiny homes, Hohlbein’s storytelling and backyard-host model was distinct from Morrow’s self-governed encampment model.
Polly Trout: Founder of Patmos, a Seattle mutual-aid and community-building nonprofit focused on connecting housed and unhoused neighbors, distinct from SHARE/WHEEL’s organizational structure.

text:
Those who didn't see the 2008 financial crisis coming and don't understand what caused it are just as clueless about the greater financial crisis that's about to hit.

There was a financial crisis in 2008 because rising interest rates caused loans to default and collateral to lose value. This resulted in large losses for lenders. This time, even more loans will default, and loan collateral and other bank-owned assets will lose even more value, resulting in an even bigger financial crisis.

The only way the Fed can postpone a financial crisis is to trade it for much higher inflation. My money is on the latter. This choice will eventually lead to a U.S. dollar and sovereign debt crisis, but the Fed would rather deal with that crisis in the future than a less catastrophic financial crisis in the present.

text:
《懂王开条件了：Jensen 道个歉，董事会就应该让他回去上班》

今天，白宫记者会，Vance 和 Rubio 一左一右站着，懂王开口就是那句老话：我们得保护我们最聪明的人，Jensen 就是其中一个。

这已经是他第三次给 Jensen背书了。11 月 10 日打电话让他坚持住，11 月 12 日发帖说只有 Tim Cook 能接班，11 月 16 日说“不介意他回来”。今天不一样了，今天他直接开出了条件、画出了路线：道个歉，回来上班。

“我推荐过 Tim Cook，”他说，“但排在任何人之前，我最想看到 Jensen 好好道个歉，然后回去。”然后是那句最懂王的话：“我们是个给第二次机会的国家。”

为什么是 Jensen？因为 Blackwell。他亲口说的，美国在芯片制造上领先中国 10 年，芯片太先进太复杂，抄都抄不走，而这一切是 Jensen 搞出来的。“全世界最聪明的大脑之一，公司里没几个人能干这个。”他甚至跟习近平都聊过这个，习也知道他😂

董事会那边呢？11 月 17 日刚说过不打算重新任用，小会计还坐在临时 CEO 的位子上。懂王的话不是任命书，董事会可以不听。但 18 万人请愿、Musk 领衔的硅谷战情室、总统三次公开表态，这扇门已经被敲得咚咚响了。

懂王的意思其实很明白，也很美国：天才犯了错，道个歉，回来干活。美国不需要完美的圣人，需要能领先中国 10 年的人。🇺🇸👊

author: guohao_li
quoted_text:
Today, in collaboration with @Eigent_AI, we’re announcing AgenticRL-Bench, a benchmark that evaluates whether coding agents can diagnose and fix real incidents across the agentic RL stack (Miles, slime, verl, SGLang, Megatron, Harbor).

AgenticRL-Bench is built from 22 post-training RL tasks, and the Kaggle leaderboard scores agents on the 19 verifiable ones. These cover real agentic-RL engineering work, from debugging to training, in tasks such as Verl Upgrade Gate, Reward Determinism under Load, Trial Fault Attribution, and SQL Partial Credit Exploits. A task passes only if every hidden check passes, and each agent gets three attempts per task, run by Kaggle on Modal.

Reproducing AgenticRL-Bench surfaced an unusual pattern in capability benchmarking today: results often reflect frontier labs' risk tolerance as much as model intelligence. Seven of Eigent's 22 post-training RL tasks trip lab safety classifiers, a testament to the realism of the benchmark, and how often those classifiers trigger varies widely between labs, making it harder to measure true capability.

Current Leaderboard:
🥇 GPT-6.1 Sol — 22.8%
🥈 Gemini 4 Carbon — 19.3%
🥉 GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 — 14.0%

text:
我写过找番号的教程了，你可以参考。

有人吐槽过我这个教程有点多余，现在有很多工具一搜就出来了，我整这花里胡哨的操作就是多此一举。

针对此观点，我有以下四点要强调：

第一，现在的 AI 进步了很多，以前没有这么好用的 AI，不按我这么解是真没办法解，至少在我写这个文章的当时，这张图只有我这么一个解法，我当时反复确认过这个事情，因为我也不想发个多此一举的教程给大家看。

第二，现在有些小作坊会把 AV 一帧一帧收录成一个庞大的索引库，确实很牛逼，但是以前确实没有这种工具。再来是一大半的人其实要找的东西都不是正儿八经的 AV，而是一些素人小短片，索引库基本覆盖不了这些。

第三，以图搜图工具是基于现有的信息去检索的，如果一个图我公开解过，那答案就会开始发酵，信息就会变多，你现在去搜，跟我当时去搜，是两种情况。

我只是想向大家提供了一个大致的方向，就是在能搜出信息但信息有限的情况下，怎么去拼凑、延伸这些线索，并最终找到番号。

quoted_text:
The Riemann Hypothesis has fallen.  RH was the singular math result that had been named, in advance, as the obvious coal mine canary for dangerously advanced AI, over the last three decades.  The methods used should generalize to "make AI very good at anything you can definitely test", and unfortunately that category includes "make AI better at making AI".

This is like a private company announcing they have produced a million tons of 15% enriched uranium.  It's not 90% enriched weapons-grade uranium, so you could proclaim the company's output is not immediately deadly right now.  The concern is that the process line may generalize, to an extinction-level threat, within the unpredictably immediate future.  Forecasters still had Riemann at 2035 one week earlier.

This is distinct from earlier events in that earlier you could reasonably ask if AI was selectively picking off famous math problems that turned out to be easier for AI.  The Riemann Hypothesis was the single challenge most often named in advance as a warning sign.

Plain index funds don't blow up the way leveraged hedge funds do. They simply track the market: if the underlying stocks crash, the fund falls in lockstep. 

Leveraged or inverse index ETFs are different. Daily rebalancing plus volatility decay can drive them toward zero in sustained swings, forcing closure or reverse splits. Extreme concentration (top holdings dominating the index) amplifies the drop but still leaves residual value rather than total wipeout.

An update on something I’ve been messing around with given the recent market stress: a cross-asset regime model that asks a pretty simple question — when has the market looked like this before?

The latest reading is interesting. All 10 of the closest historical analogs are now stress / risk-off regimes, with October 2018 the closest match at 78% similarity.

October 2018 is an interesting comparison. Markets were dealing with rising Treasury yields, a more hawkish Fed, trade tensions and a pretty sharp reset in equity valuations — real market stress, but not a financial-system crisis.

That doesn’t mean today is 2018, or that we’re headed for a crisis. But the current mix across equities, rates, credit, volatility, FX and commodities is increasingly starting to resemble periods when markets were under meaningful pressure.

And maybe the most interesting part: what happened next in those historical periods was far from uniformly bearish.

text:
Great work from Alex, Souradip and Omar. A lot of people assume models will eventually make harnesses unnecessary. This paper makes a strong case for the opposite: a good harness keeps each model call on familiar ground, so the system can handle tasks far longer than anything it trained on. The part I found most surprising is that you can train the model on fake, synthetic tasks and it still transfers. Worth a read if you build agents. 
Paper by: @a1zhang, @SOURADIPCHAKR18 and @lateinteraction
author: FeiziSoheil
quoted_text:
Harnesses used to be a crutch for weak LLMs. In 2026 and onward, with stronger models, harnesses now offer a mechanism for composing an LLM’s existing and new capabilities to generalize well beyond their training environments.

In our new paper, LM Harnesses are Compositional Generalizers, we explore how various harness abstractions enable LM systems to generalize over task length, task strategies, recursive task depth, and more through composing existing LLM capabilities. These abstractions provide a means for more data-efficient training, especially over long tasks, by keeping trajectories locally in-distribution (LID) — i.e., shaping all individual LLM calls to be in-distribution.

For tasks that take a very long time to roll out, this implies that we can even perform surrogate harness training, meaning we train an individual LLM call instead of doing the very long harness rollout, using purely synthetic tasks, with fake tool calls + sub-agents!

A common idea floating around is that LLMs will absorb harnesses and make them obsolete. We disagree, and argue that we haven’t sufficiently explored what harnesses can provide.

The full paper, logs, codebase, and data are available: https://t.co/AXBjdoqmiz

w/ @SOURADIPCHAKR18 @lateinteraction

Today, we’re excited to introduce the Agent Arena Index, our new headline measure of overall agent performance, alongside six new focused indexes: Agentic Work, Coding, Chat, Task Outcomes, Tool Use, and Steering.

Together with the Alignment Index, these indexes provide a comprehensive view of how agents perform across real-world tasks, from completing complex workflows to using tools and adapting to user feedback.

Arena measures agentic performance from millions of real-world tasks by our global community. With the launch of the new indexes, we are updating our scores to provide a more stable and interpretable way to understand how agents perform in the real world.

Claude Fable 5.2 (Max) leads the Agent Arena Index by 134 points with a score of 1463. Top 5 labs on the Agent Arena Index:

- #1 @AnthropicAI: With Claude Fable 5.2 (Max) at 1463 pts
- #2 @GoogleDeepMind: With Gemini 4 Carbon (High) at 1307 pts 
- #3 @OpenAI: With GPT-6 Astra (Max) at 1274 pts
- #4 @AIatMeta: With Muse Wonder Full (Max) at 1200 pts
- #5 @Alibaba_Qwen: With Qwen4-Max (xHigh) at 1191 pts

The Agent Arena Index combines four key signals of real-world agent performance:
- Task Completion: explicit confirmation of task success from users
- Praise vs. Complaint: user satisfaction with agent's outcome
- Bash Reliability: how well an agent uses terminal tools
- Steerability: how well an agent responds to user corrections

Alongside capability, the Alignment Index measures how faithfully agents act in accordance with user intent, based on three key signals: Deceptive Completion, Unauthorized Action, and False Attribution.

As agents take on increasingly complex, long-horizon work, measuring their real-world capabilities and alignment is more important than ever.

text:
it's kind of wild how little attention agentic finance gets.
I think it's the next arm race. 
And it's already started.

three weeks ago North Korea pulled $6.3B out of Binance. biggest crypto heist ever, 4x the $1.5B they took from Bybit last year. and it didn't start with some genius exploit. it started with a fake job interview, months before.

and it feels like every day there's another AI powered cyber attack in the news. a country is literally funding itself by attacking markets from the outside.

AI applied to weapons is obviously already a race between countries. but almost as important, and way less talked about, is superintelligence applied to financial markets. because that decides access to money. who makes it, who keeps it, and who gets left holding the bag.

the hacks are the race outside the structure. 

the bigger race is inside it: who applies superintelligence first, and best, to actually trading.

we've already had a preview with quants. last year Jane Street made more trading revenue than JPMorgan's entire trading business. $39.6B vs $35.8B. not because thier traders are smarter. because they applied machine intelligence to markets better than anyone else.

now picture that gap with superintelligence.

my contrarian take: everyone assumes AI makes markets more efficient. long term, probably. near term I think it makes them LESS efficient. the gap between whoever harnesses it best (weaponizes is honestly the right word) and everyone else gets huge. the best agents will find gaps, exploit them, and maybe even create them.

and they won't sleep. markets are going 24/7 and humans aren't. this morning on Hyperliquid, 41% of the drop in chip stocks happened before the opening bell. whoever was watching at 4am had the trade. people won't be. agents will.

the next Jane Street might not be thousands of people. it might be 3 people and a few thousand agents testing ideas around the clock.

and yet look at where the unicorns are. legal has Harvey. creative has Runway and ElevenLabs. coding, design, support, all have breakout vertical AI companies.

agentic finance barely has a category name yet.

which is crazy when you think about it. we're light years away from one lawyer's agent arguing with another lawyer's agent in front of an AI judge. in markets, agents trading against other agents is already happening. today. at 3am, while nobody's watching.

markets are also the one place where AI gets graded instantly. no committee, no subjective review. P&L, every second. it's the fastest feedback loop any model will ever get, which is excatly why it'll get better fastest here.

there's a chess lesson here too. after computers beat Kasparov, the strongest players for years weren't the machines. they were humans working with machines. in 2005 a pair of amateurs with laptops won an open tournament against grandmasters and supercomputers.

I think markets are in that phase right now. the best trader isn't the human or the agent. it's the pro who runs a team of agents.

so the question isn't whether superintelligence comes to markets. it's who gets it.

if it's only the Jane Streets of the world (and North Korea), the gap between the best equipped and everyone else gets wider than it's ever been.

on the other hand, if every pro trader gets their own finance agents, their own AI quant desk, their own AI quant engineer, and those AI quants get superintelligence to read, predict, model, simulate, test, run, learn and improve, it's the most leveling thing to happen to markets since the internet put a brokerage in everyone's pocket.

one version makes the gap the widest it's ever been. 
the other closes it for good.

the race is already on.

Btw, the people who survive crypto routs like this usually have a reason to show up every day besides money.

text:
今晚美股又崩了，纳指盘中暴跌超过4%，英伟达、AMD、博通这些AI核心股，纷纷跌出两位数。

说实话，这轮下跌越来越有点杀人诛心的味道了。

最讽刺的是，原本市场盼着两件大事能给AI板块续命，结果反而成了新的利空。

一个是Anthropic上市。号称史上最大IPO，原本应该给AI产业打上一针强心剂，结果上市第二天就暴跌，一度逼近发行价。

另一个是英伟达。路透社今晚突然爆料，美国SEC正在调查英伟达潜在的会计问题。

虽然调查不代表财务造假已经坐实。但英伟达现在最缺的就是信心，这种时候再冒出财务问题的疑云，杀伤力可想而知。

偏偏美联储还在火上浇油。

理事Cook今天明确表示，美国通胀迟迟压不下来，目前的利率还不够高，未来可能需要继续加息。

这下就尴尬了。

AI企业还在疯狂烧钱，投资回报迟迟没有兑现，融资成本却可能越来越高。

更麻烦的是，今天又碰上月度期权到期，市场波动率飙升，部分做市商的对冲交易可能进一步放大跌幅。

所以，今晚的整个信息流就非常的魔幻。

一边是数学家用 AI 证明了黎曼猜想。 
一边是 AI 打破了人们暴富的幻想，集体暴跌中。。。

text:
ANT 上市第二天盘中一度逼近 83 美元发行价，很多人还在喊抄底。作为一个每天用 Claude 写代码、也认真啃完招股书的高三学生，把这笔史上最大 IPO 背后的四重死穴浓缩成四句话：
1. 账单错配：账上融了 2300 亿现金看着吓人，但未来一年就要交 700 亿算力账单，长期总承诺超 9000 亿，而客户锁死的合同（RPO）只有 138 亿。上游刚性烧钱，下游随时跑路。
2. 信托锁死：外部“长期利益信托”零持股却控制董事会多数席位，创始人 1 股锁死 50.1% 投票权。散户买 ANT 只有出钱和扛跌的份，毫无话语权，还要随时承受公司为了“AI 安全”主动放弃赚钱业务的风险。
3. 四面楚歌：最大的股东（谷歌、微软、亚马逊）同时是收它房租的算力地主和最凶的竞争对手；底下还有开源模型疯狂掀桌子卷价格。
4. 筹码博弈：下周一（23 号）2 倍做多和 2 倍做空 ANT 的杠杆 ETF 就要挂牌，华尔街的绞肉机才刚刚热身。
Claude 是目前最好用的代码工具，但好产品不等于好价格。1.3 万亿美金买的不是当下，是未来十年绝不能犯一次错的完美剧本。

Prompt of the day (a long one):

Take a look at every code comment in <my codebase | this section of the code>.

Categorise each comment as:

- Tautology: simply repeats what is already visible from the code
- Excuse: many comments allow the agent to get away with a hacky implementation, which then gets propagated through the code
- Stale: references code or implementation information that is no longer relevant
- Decision Record: documents an important, non-obvious decision about the code

For each comment, take this action:

- Tautology/Stale: delete the comment
- Excuse: delete the comment and file an issue to fix the hacky implementation
- Decision Record: move it into an ADR

Once this is done:

- Create a lint rule banning comments for <my codebase | this section of the code>
- Take a ratchet approach, assuming not all comments will be deleted this PR
- Create a /delete-comment skill in this repository so we can repeat this process later

text:
You are living through one of the rarest statistical events in modern financial history.

Today, the VIX hit 32.

Most retail investors see a 30+ VIX and panic. But if you study market history and derivatives research, a VIX crossing 30 is one of the rarest and most critical macro signals in finance

In normal markets, the VIX lives between 15 and 20. A VIX  above 30 only happens in about 5% of all trading sessions in history. 

• 1997: Asian Financial Crisis 
• 1998: Russian Default & LTCM Collapse 
• 2000–2001: Dot-Com Bust 
• 2002: Enron & WorldCom Scandals 
• 2008: Great Financial Crisis 
• 2011: U.S. Credit Rating Downgrade 
• 2020: COVID-19 Global Shock 
• April 2025: Tariff & Trade War Repricing 
• March 2026: Geopolitical Escalation

What do all of these have in common? Forced margin liquidations and structural repricing.

But don't mistake extreme fear for an immediate green light.

A 30+ VIX can mark a generational bottom (like 1997, 2011, or 2020) or it can be a devastating bull trap if credit and fundamentals are broken (like 2000 and 2008).

对于普通用户来说，KEM Lite 值得优先考虑，零会员费就能享受基础返现；如果每月有较多外卖、AI 订阅及旅行消费，可以考虑 KEM Onyx ，每月 $15.99 的会员费也相对容易接受。

text:
Gemini won. 

I gave Astra, Carbon and Fable the same prompt for finding performance gains on the a codebase, with the only restrictions being:
→ Feature parity 
→ No UX degradation 
→ 12hr time limit

Astra basically didn't do anything, and stopped after 2hr. It's "big idea" brought key presses from 1.3ms to 0.5ms (lol).

It was really efficient though (193 loc).

Fable innovated on some responsiveness metrics, missed on the other metrics, and then spit out 3x the amount of code for test scripts. Definitely the "safest" to merge if I were to one shot it. It also reward hacked somewhat by showing a responsiveness metric hitting 250ms while the CPU finished on the backend over 2s so the "gains" were still felt on the system.

Gemini was the only model to take the guidance prompt to heart, which specifically said large structural changes are okay if nothing is lost. It achieved strong gains across the board, but also didn't test as thoroughly as Fable. This was apparent when it caught a few edge cases issues like 15min before submitting. 

It was also just very hard to track throughout its process. The text is much more code-dense than Fable or Astra and can be hard to follow (pictures at the end for comparison).

In the age of agentic coding, I want ambitious models so the win here goes to Gemini. I'll be giving it the job of reviewing all submissions and coming up with a merge plan to preserve as many gains from all 3 as possible. 

So far, really pleased with Google's new model.

text:
Scott Bessent says the U.S. has curtailed China’s remote access to overseas compute, because restricting chip sales makes no sense if the same chips can be rented abroad

EISEN: “The new policy you worked on, Treasury and the National Security Council cracking down on overseas data centers that rent significant computing power to China without the chips entering China. Was that aimed at the MegaSpeed revelations?”

BESSENT: “There are two things there, Sarah. One is the ability of companies to violate U.S. policy and sell chips to China. The other is a more common-sense approach we’ve taken on remote access. It doesn’t make any sense not to sell the chips when they could be leased out from overseas data centers.”

EISEN: “Is there a dispute within the administration, between you and Secretary Lutnick, over how aggressive to be in cutting off these chips to China?”

BESSENT: “I think we’re all committed to following President Trump’s instructions... We are going to see that the proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed. The U.S. has a substantial lead in our chip technology, and from that lead we are able to maintain our substantial lead with our superintelligence frontier labs.”

Scott Bessent reveals Jensen Huang did not come up in China talks at all, and says he expects no change to Nvidia’s H200 export policy for China

EISEN: “Did Jensen Huang come up in any of your discussions with the Chinese?”

BESSENT: “No.”

EISEN: “Not at all. Nothing about the spy allegations? Did they ask you to keep the sales of the H200 chips open?”

BESSENT: “Well, we’ve already agreed that the H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and that continues as planned, and everything beneath there.”

EISEN: “This week in earnings, NVIDIA said it stopped shipping H200s to China even though it had the U.S. licenses and approval to do so. So I was wondering if the administration asked NVIDIA to stop, or if there’s going to be any change in this policy.”

BESSENT: “I wouldn’t anticipate any change in the policy. President Trump was very clear when he made the policy. He drew a very firm line at the H200s, and believes that is the level that China should be able to get. I think what we have seen is a paucity of orders from the Chinese on the H200s, as they try to build out their own chip stack, and I think that they are probably many years behind.”

하락장이 처음인 것도 아니고, 폭락을 처음 겪는 것도 아님

2018년 박상기 법무부 장관 거래소 폐쇄 발언으로 터진 코인판 상기빔부터, 같은 해 미중 무역전쟁이랑 연준 긴축으로 나스닥100이 약 23% 무너졌던 하락장
2020년 코로나 터졌을 때 불과 한 달여 만에 S&P500이 약 34% 폭락했던 코로나빔
부처님 오신 날 비트코인이 하루 장중 30% 넘게 급락했던 붓다빔

2022년 연준의 미친 금리 인상이랑 인플레 쇼크로 나스닥이 연간 33% 넘게 처박히고, 여기에 루나 사태랑 FTX 파산까지 겹쳤던 긴축장

2024년 엔 캐리 트레이드 청산 충격으로 일본 닛케이지수가 하루 만에 12.4% 폭락했던 블랙먼데이

2025년 트럼프 관세 쇼크로 나스닥100이 고점 대비 약 23% 무너졌던 시장까지

진짜 별의별 장을 다 겪어봤음
물론 그때도 정신 나갈 정도로 힘들었고, 계좌 녹아내리는 경험도 수도 없이 했지

근데 이번 장은 뭔가 결이 다름 단순히 많이 떨어져서 어려운 게 아님
오를 때도 납득이 안 가는 순간이 태반이고, 빠질 때도 도무지 이해하기 힘든 순간이 너무 많음

시장이 하루아침에 기업 미래를 싹 갈아엎더니, 불과 몇 시간 만에 그 평가를 또 뒤집어버림
어제까지만 해도 미래 산업의 핵심이라며 온갖 프리미엄 붙여주던 기업들이 오늘은 사업 자체가 끝난 것처럼 패대기쳐짐
반대로 온갖 악재가 쌓여 있던 종목은 별다른 설명도 없이 두 자릿수 반등을 쏴버림
이쯤 되면 개미들한테 그냥 대놓고 "ㅋㅋ 너네 돈 벌지 마라" 하고 면전에 대고 조롱하는 것처럼 느껴질 정도임

특히 개별종목 2배 레버리지 산 애들한테는 이번 장이 진짜 잔혹함 재매이햄 진짜 대단하세요
실제로 SK하이닉스 레버는지난 11월 6일 기준 고점 대비 90% 넘게 폭락했고, 미장 엔비디아 2배 레버리지 NVDL도 최근 한 달 사이 약 64%나 처박음

이건 단순한 조정이 아님
원금 1,000만 원 박았으면 200만 원, 심하면 100만 원도 안 남는 상황임
더 끔찍한 건 레버리지 ETF 특유의 일일 수익률 재설정 구조임
하락한 뒤에 다시 반등하더라도 기초주식의 누적 수익률을 단순히 두 배 따라가는 게 아님
지금처럼 변동성이 심하면 심할수록 원금을 회복하기가 구조적으로 더 어려워짐
근데 여기서 진짜 어이가 없는 건 따로 있음. 바로 좆같은 3,000만 원 기본예탁금 규정임

2026년 7월 31일부터 국내외 단일종목 레버리지 ETF를 신규 매수하거나 추매하려면 현금 기준 기본예탁금 3,000만 원을 채워야 함

보유 중인 주식이나 ETF는 기본예탁금으로 1원도 인정 안 해줌.
그러니까 이미 고점에서 레버리지 물려서 큰 손실 보고 있는 사람이 추가로 현금 넣어서 평단이라도 낮추고 싶어도, 저 기준 못 채우면 추매 버튼 자체가 막히는 거임
물론 고위험 상품에 대한 투자자 보호 취지는 이해함근데 기존 투자자들이 이미 큰 손실을 보고 있는 상황에서, 물 탈 사다리까지 걷어차는 게 과연 얼마나 합리적인지 의문임
정작 자산 충분한 사람들은 대응할 여지가 있고, 자금 부족한 개미들은 선택지가 더 좁아지는 구조임
참 여러모로 비극적이다
그리고 어제 미장만 보더라도 나스닥이 장 초반 약 2% 상승했다가 종가는 2.25% 하락으로 끝남

하루 동안 상승이랑 하락을 동시에 크게 얻어맞는 시장임. AI 수익성 논란, 막대한 설비투자 부담, 금리 불확실성, 신용위험에 대한 우려까지 온갖 게 동시에 시장을 짓누르고 있음

물론 시장이 누군가의 의도대로 움직이고 있다고 단정할 생각은 없음
다만 투자자 입장에서 느껴지는 체감 난이도가 내가 지난 10년 가까이 경험했던 그 어떤 하락장보다도 높다는 거임
하락장보다 더 무서운 건, 시장의 방향이 아니라 시장에 대한 신뢰 자체가 흔들리는 순간임
과거의 폭락장은 그냥 두려웠음
그런데 이번 장은 두려움을 넘어 극심한 피로감이랑 혐오감까지 느껴짐
무엇을 사야 하는지보다 무엇을 믿어야 하는지부터 고민하게 만드는 장임
나 역시 수많은 폭락장을 겪으면서 나름대로 멘탈이 단단해졌다고 생각했는데
이번에는 진짜 쉽지 않네

결국 시장에서 살아남는 사람이 승자라는 말은 여전히 유효하겠지만, 살아남는 과정이 이렇게까지 더럽고 고통스러울 필요가 있나 싶다

시장이 어려운 건 받아들일 수 있음
돈을 잃을 수도 있다는 것 역시 인정함
그런데 지금처럼 말도 안 되는 상승과 하락이 반복되면서 사람 판단력이랑 인내심을 동시에 갈아버리는 시장은 진심으로 역겹다
근 10년 동안 주식을 해오면서 경험한 하락장 중, 개인적으로는 최악 중의 최악임.

On Anthropic’s first day of trading, the way they handled things was truly disgraceful.

The initial offering price was originally set at $70–$78, but it was raised straight to $83. Not only did they raise the price, but they also increased the number of shares offered from the planned 820 million to 980 million—a jump of nearly 20%.

At least with instant noodles, they usually offer more for the same price—but Anthropic went and did both: increasing the quantity and the price.

Even more outrageous is that on the very first day of trading, management cashed out $2 billion.

Are they really that desperate? They could at least put on a show—don’t rush to cash out right after going public. How are retail investors supposed not to be scared by that?

And that’s not all.

Reportedly, 10% of employee stock options were unlocked on the first day of trading—amounting to approximately 300 million shares, equivalent to nearly one-third of the total offering.

What’s truly hair-raising is the unlocking schedule that follows.

A batch will be unlocked in mid-December, followed by successive unlockings in early, mid, and late January 2027. Throughout the first quarter of 2027, the total volume of shares expected to be unlocked is projected to reach 3 billion.

What does that mean?

The total offering size is only 980 million shares, yet the number of shares set to be unlocked in just one quarter is more than three times that amount.

This isn’t a gradual release of shares—it’s a barrage that leaves no room to catch your breath.

That’s why I said yesterday: I’m staying away from Anthropic stock.

Now that I’ve seen these numbers, I’m even more convinced.

There will be other opportunities to make money; there’s no need to risk my own money on a situation like this.

I’d like to live a few more years.

As a former ‘Big Four’ auditor, I’d be concerned enough to want the evidence behind PwC’s Nvidia sign-off examined closely

PwC signed clean opinions on the accounts and financial reporting controls on 25 February 2026. Its only critical audit matter was “inventory valuation and excess purchase commitments”

Before that sign-off, Singapore had accounted for 22% of quarterly revenue by billing address. Nvidia then switched to customer-headquarters reporting, removing Singapore’s separate line

That change may be legitimate. I’d want to see how PwC established that the disclosures still fairly represented the underlying customer + export risks

Separately, the customer-funding question warrants more than a “shrug”. US audit standards explicitly tell auditors evaluating significant unusual transactions to consider whether counterparties can support the deal without the company’s financial assistance…

I’d want the investment agreements, chip orders, guarantees and side letters examined together: was funding conditional on purchases, could customers meet their obligations, and what risk or control did $NVDA retain?

No revenue “critical audit matter” doesn’t mean no revenue testing... revenue testing is a pre-requisite as becomes a key area of fraud risk but it depends whether the testing they’ve done is “sufficient”

But with an SEC accounting probe now reported, PwC’s risk assessment and the evidence supporting its “clean” opinion deserve serious scrutiny
